title: What literature is
description: Literature, from Latin littera ("letter"), means written works, above all imaginative poetry and prose, but scholars also speak of oral literature.

facts.text: The word literature comes from the Latin littera, "a letter of the alphabet".
In its simplest definition literature is a body of written works, but the name usually means imaginative poetry and prose valued for the quality of their making.
Scholars also speak of oral literature, the literature of peoples without writing, so literature is not only written.

title: From spoken stories to the novel
description: Literature ran from spoken myths to writing on clay (about 5,200 years ago), to epics like Gilgamesh and Homer, to the novel (Genji, about 1010).

facts.text: Cuneiform, the earliest confirmed writing, was pressed into clay tablets by the Sumerians of southern Mesopotamia from about the end of the 4th millennium BCE, about 5,200 years ago.
Five short Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh survive on clay tablets written in the first half of the 2nd millennium BCE.
Homer is thought to have lived in the 9th or 8th century BCE, and his epics grew out of a centuries-old tradition of singers composing orally.
Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji, finished about 1010, is often called the world's first novel.
An epic is a long narrative poem recounting heroic deeds.
A novel is an invented prose story of considerable length and complexity; unlike the epic, it often shows life as unheroic, imperfect, even absurd.

title: Fables and Aesop
description: A fable is a short tale, usually with animals acting like people, that carries a moral; the best known are credited to Aesop, a likely legendary Greek.

facts.text: In the fable of the Fox and the Grapes, a fox jumps again and again for grapes he cannot reach, then walks off calling them sour grapes, not worth the trouble.
The phrase "sour grapes" comes from the fable, ascribed to Aesop, of the fox who called the grapes he could not reach sour.
A fable usually features animals that talk and act like humans, pokes at human follies, and carries a moral that is often stated at the end.
The moral of the Fox and the Grapes in The Aesop for Children (1919) reads: "There are many who pretend to despise and belittle that which is beyond their reach."
Aesop is a likely legendary figure; the earliest known collection of fables under his name dates to the 4th century BCE.

title: Myth, legend and folk tale
description: A myth is a traditional symbolic story tied to religious belief; a legend is told as history about a particular person or place; folk tales are found everywhere and change with each teller.

facts.text: In the scholarly sense, a myth is a symbolic, traditional story, usually of unknown origin, told as if its events really happened and tied to religious belief; it does not mean a falsehood.
A legend is a traditional story about a particular person or place, told as a matter of history.
William Tell, Switzerland's legendary hero of freedom, is said to have shot an apple from his son's head, but there is no evidence that he existed.
Folk tales are found almost everywhere, include fairy tales and nursery tales, and keep changing as tellers pass them on.

title: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk
description: The Epic of Gilgamesh, often cited as the earliest significant surviving literature, follows a king of Uruk and his friend Enkidu; its fullest text is on 12 clay tablets from Nineveh.

facts.text: The Epic of Gilgamesh, about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk in Mesopotamia, is often cited as the earliest significant work of literature to survive.
The real Gilgamesh probably ruled Uruk, in southern Mesopotamia, sometime in the first half of the 3rd millennium BCE.
In the epic, the gods create Enkidu, a wild man living among animals, to restrain Gilgamesh; after a trial of strength the two become close friends.
Together Gilgamesh and Enkidu kill Humbaba, guardian of a remote cedar forest, and the Bull of Heaven.
The fullest text of the epic is on 12 incomplete clay tablets in Akkadian, found at Nineveh in the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal.

title: Gilgamesh's search to escape death
description: After Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh seeks the flood survivor Utnapishtim to escape death, wins a plant of youth, loses it to a serpent and returns to Uruk still mortal.

facts.text: The gods decide that Enkidu must die for killing the Bull of Heaven, and his death hits Gilgamesh hard.
Gilgamesh makes a dangerous journey to find Utnapishtim, the survivor of the great flood, to learn from him how to escape death.
Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh where to find a plant that renews youth; Gilgamesh gets it, a serpent seizes it, and he returns to Uruk still mortal.

title: George Smith and the flood tablet
description: In 1872 George Smith, a self-taught former banknote engraver at the British Museum, recognized a flood story on the 11th tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh.

facts.text: According to a later account by E. A. Wallis Budge, George Smith, on reading the flood tablet in 1872, jumped up and rushed about the room in great excitement, and began to undress.
George Smith was apprenticed as a banknote engraver at 14, taught himself to read cuneiform, and was hired to work on tablets at the British Museum.
Smith wrote that his eye caught the statement that the ship rested on the mountains of Nizir, followed by a dove sent out that found no resting place and returned.
The flood story Smith found is on the 11th tablet of the 12-tablet Epic of Gilgamesh.
Smith presented his discovery to the Society of Biblical Archaeology in 1872, with Prime Minister Gladstone in the audience.
The Daily Telegraph then paid for an expedition to Nineveh, where in May 1873 Smith found a fragment he believed completed the flood account.

title: The Babylonian flood and Genesis
description: The flood in Gilgamesh shares its shape with the flood of Genesis (a divinely ordered boat, animals, a mountain, birds), but differs in cause and outcome.

facts.text: In the Babylonian flood story, Utnapishtim builds a vessel at a god's command, takes animals aboard, grounds on Mount Nimush and sends out a dove, a swallow and a raven.
In Genesis, God tells Noah to build an ark and take male and female of every animal; the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat, and Noah sends out a raven and a dove.
Scholars see Babylonian flood traditions as the source of features of the biblical story, such as building and stocking the ark and the waters going down.
In the Babylonian story the flood comes from a disagreement among the gods, in Genesis from human wrongdoing; Utnapishtim joins the immortal gods, while Noah's family renews history.

title: Shapes of creation stories
description: Creation myths tell how the world began; common shapes include order out of chaos (Enuma Elish, Hesiod) and the cosmic egg (Pan Gu).

facts.text: A creation myth is a symbolic story of how the world began and how people first came to live in it.
The Babylonian Enuma Elish begins with a watery chaos with no sky or land, where the sea goddess Tiamat and the sweet-water god Apsu mingle their waters.
In the Enuma Elish, the god Marduk defeats Tiamat and cuts her body in two, making the earth from one half and the heavens from the other.
The Enuma Elish was recited during Akitu, the Babylonian New Year festival.
In Hesiod's Theogony, as Hugh G. Evelyn-White translated it: "Verily at the first Chaos came to be."
The birth of the world from a cosmic egg is a widespread motif in myth.

In Chinese creation stories, Pan Gu came out of chaos, an egg, and separated heaven and earth; another telling makes the world from his body, his eyes becoming the sun and moon and his blood the rivers.
The Pan Gu creation myths date from the 3rd to the 6th century.

title: The earth diver
description: In earth-diver myths an animal dives into primal water to bring up earth; in the Haudenosaunee story, a muskrat's bit of earth grows on a turtle's back into North America.

facts.text: The earth-diver myth is widely distributed around the world.
The Haudenosaunee tell of Sky Woman, who fell from the Sky World toward the water; birds caught her and set her on the back of a great turtle.
In the Haudenosaunee story, animals dove for earth; the muskrat came up with a little earth in his claws, and on the turtle's back it grew into North America, Turtle Island.

title: Homer's formulas
description: Oral poets composed with formulas, ready-made phrases like "rosy-fingered dawn" shaped to fit the meter; Parry recorded a singer who could not read performing about 12,000 lines.

facts.text: In Samuel Butler's translation of the Odyssey, the line "the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn" recurs again and again.
Oral epic poets used verbal formulas, refined over generations to fit the meter, to compose and remember long poems.
Phrases like "rosy-fingered dawn" and "wine-dark sea" are formulas: they fit set places in Homer's meter, the dactylic hexameter, so a singer could compose without stopping.
In the 1930s Milman Parry transcribed an epic of about 12,000 lines from a singer in Yugoslavia who could not read.
Parry and his student Albert Lord recorded oral poets composing in performance in Yugoslavia.
Many scholars think writing, through dictation, transcription or later editing, helped turn fluid oral performances into the stable texts of Homer we read.

title: Type-scenes
description: Homeric singers also inherited type-scenes, recurring story blocks with a set structure (a sacrifice, welcoming a guest, launching a ship, arming), and reshaped them in performance.

facts.text: A type-scene is a recurring block of story with a set structure, such as a sacrifice, welcoming a guest, launching a ship or a warrior putting on armor.
Homer's epics grew from a centuries-old tradition in which singers inherited phrases, scenes and plots and reshaped them in performance, composing orally.

title: Ovid's Metamorphoses
description: Ovid finished the Metamorphoses, 15 books of Latin hexameter, about 8 CE; its stories, from the creation to Julius Caesar, all involve a transformation.

facts.text: Daphne refused every suitor, Apollo included; when the god chased her she prayed for rescue and was turned into a laurel, which Apollo took for poets and Roman triumphs.
Daphne's transformation into a laurel is one of the stories in Ovid's Metamorphoses.
Ovid finished the Metamorphoses, a poem in 15 books of Latin hexameter verse, about 8 CE.

The Metamorphoses collects myths, many from Greek sources, in which a transformation plays a part, told in order from the creation of the world (chaos turned to order) to the death and deification of Julius Caesar.
In 8 CE, just as the Metamorphoses was complete, the emperor banished Ovid to Tomis.

Ovid tells of Pyramus and Thisbe, Babylonian lovers forbidden to marry who talk through a crack in the wall; Thisbe flees a lioness and drops her veil, Pyramus thinks her dead and kills himself, and she follows.
In Ovid's telling, the mulberry tree's snow-white fruit is dyed dark purple by Pyramus's blood.

title: Ovid's influence
description: Ovid gave scores of Greek legends the form later generations knew; from the 15th to 17th centuries nearly every poet and painter of note owed him something, Shakespeare included.

facts.text: Ovid gave scores of Greek legends their definitive form for later generations.
In the 15th to 17th centuries it would be hard to name a poet or painter of note who did not owe something to Ovid.
In Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, workmen act a farcical Pyramus and Thisbe, and the tale was one inspiration for Romeo and Juliet.

title: Hou Yi and the ten suns
description: In Chinese myth, ten suns burned the earth until the archer Hou Yi shot down nine of them (one account says 8 of 9).

facts.text: In Chinese myth, the archer Hou Yi shot down 9 of 10 suns that were burning up the earth; one account says 8 of 9.
Hou Yi is the Lord Archer of Chinese myth, whose skill with a bow earned him undying fame; he is best known as the husband of Chang'e.

title: Chang'e and the Moon
description: Chang'e swallowed the elixir of immortality her husband Yi received from the Queen Mother of the West and fled to the Moon; the Mid-Autumn Festival honors her.

facts.text: Yi received an elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West; before he could take it, his wife Chang'e swallowed it, became immortal and, fearing his anger, fled to the Moon's Palace of Boundless Cold.
In paintings, a white rabbit beside Chang'e on the Moon prepares the elixir of immortality with a mortar and pestle.
On the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, people celebrate Chang'e with the Mid-Autumn Festival and eat mooncakes, rich pastries with sweet or savory fillings.
Some people look for the outline of a toad on the Moon, because in one legend Chang'e became a toad.

title: Japan's Kojiki
description: The Kojiki, the oldest surviving book from Japan, was compiled in 712: Hieda no Are memorized old myths and records, and Ō no Yasumaro wrote them down.

facts.text: The Kojiki (Record of Ancient Matters), compiled in 712, is the oldest surviving text of any kind from Japan.
Emperor Temmu had a court attendant, Hieda no Are, memorize Japan's earliest myths and records; the courtier Ō no Yasumaro wrote them down and presented the Kojiki to the empress in 712.
The Kojiki was written using Chinese characters.
Much of Shinto thought is based on interpretations of the myths in the Kojiki.

title: Amaterasu in the cave
description: The sun goddess Amaterasu hid in a cave after her brother Susanoo's outrages, darkening the world, until the gods drew her out with a mirror, a dance and laughter.

facts.text: Amaterasu is the sun goddess of Shinto, from whom the Japanese imperial family claims descent.
Her brother Susanoo, the storm god, broke down the divisions in her rice fields, defiled her home and threw a flayed horse into her weaving hall.
Amaterasu withdrew into a cave in protest, and darkness fell upon the world.
The gods hung a mirror and jewels on a sakaki tree outside the cave; the goddess Amenouzume danced, the gods laughed loudly, and Amaterasu was drawn out.
The gods then threw a shimenawa, a sacred rope of rice straw, across the cave entrance so she could not hide again.
At the Grand Shrine of Ise, Amaterasu is present in a mirror that is one of the three Imperial Treasures of Japan.

title: Ashurbanipal's library
description: Ashurbanipal's scribes collected and copied ancient texts at Nineveh; when the city was sacked in 612 BCE the ruined walls buried the clay tablets, which were dug up in the mid-1800s.

facts.text: In the 7th century BCE the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal had his scribes collect and copy ancient texts of every kind, including prayers, fables and epics, for his library at Nineveh.
In 612 BCE an alliance including Babylonians and Medes sacked Nineveh, and the ruined walls buried the library's clay tablets.
Austen Henry Layard (from 1845) and then Hormuzd Rassam (from 1852) dug up the tablets, and more than 20,000 tablets and fragments went to the British Museum.

title: Odin, Thor and Loki
description: Odin (war, poets, wisdom bought with an eye), Thor (thunder, the hammer Mjollnir, Thursday) and Loki (the shape-shifting trickster behind Balder's death) are the best-known Norse gods.

facts.text: Thor was equated with the Roman Jupiter, so dies Jovis (Jove's day) became Thor's day: Thursday.
Thor, a god of all the early Germanic peoples, took his name from the Germanic word for thunder, and his hammer stood for the thunderbolt.
Odin, one of the principal Norse gods, was from earliest times a war god and protector of heroes, and also the god of poets and a great magician.
Fallen warriors joined Odin in Valhalla, his hall in Asgard.
Odin has only one eye: he gave the other in exchange for wisdom.
Thor was a red-bearded warrior of enormous strength, an enemy of giants but kind to humans.
Thor's hammer, Mjollnir, returns to the thrower like a boomerang.
Loki is a cunning trickster who can change his shape and sex; his father was a giant, yet he counts among the gods as a companion of Odin and Thor.
Loki was the principal cause of the death of the god Balder, and as punishment he was bound to a rock.

title: The two Eddas
description: Most of what we know of Norse myth comes from two Icelandic books: the Poetic Edda (poems composed 800 to 1100, copied in the 13th century) and Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda (about 1220), a handbook for poets.

facts.text: Together the two Eddas are the fullest and most detailed source for modern knowledge of Germanic mythology.
The Poetic Edda gathers mythological and heroic poems composed between 800 and 1100, in a manuscript from the second half of the 13th century.
Snorri Sturluson, an Icelandic poet, historian and chieftain, wrote the Prose Edda about 1220.
The Prose Edda is a textbook on poetics, written to teach young poets the difficult meters of the early Icelandic court poets and the myths their poems allude to.

title: Ragnarok, the end of the gods
description: In Ragnarok, the Norse end of the world, a three-year winter comes, the monsters break free, Fenrir swallows Odin, Thor and the serpent kill each other, and the earth sinks into the sea.

facts.text: Ragnarok, in Scandinavian mythology, is the end of the world of gods and men.
Ragnarok is told in the Voluspa, a 10th-century Icelandic poem, and in Snorri Sturluson's 13th-century Prose Edda.
Ragnarok begins with the Fimbulwinter, the "Mighty Winter", which lasts three years.
At Ragnarok the great wolf Fenrir and Jormungand, the Midgard serpent, are freed, and Loki escapes and steers Naglfar, a ship made of the nails of dead men.
In the last battle Fenrir swallows Odin, and Thor kills the serpent Jormungand but dies of its poison.
Surtr, the fire giant, leads the sons of Muspelheim across Bifrost and shatters the rainbow bridge.
At Ragnarok the sun turns black and the earth sinks into the sea.

title: After Ragnarok, a new world
description: Ragnarok is not the last word: the earth rises again, two humans, Lif and Lifthrasir, come out of the world-tree, and surviving gods, Balder among them, make a new home.

facts.text: After Ragnarok the earth rises again from the sea, and a woman and a man, Lif and Lifthrasir, emerge from the world-tree.
Balder is among the gods who survive Ragnarok and make a new dwelling in the renewed world.

title: The sagas of Icelanders
description: A saga is any prose story or history in medieval Icelandic. The sagas of Icelanders, written down in the 13th century by unknown authors, tell of farming families in Iceland from 930 to 1030.

facts.text: In medieval Icelandic literature, a saga is any kind of story or history in prose.
Where the kings' sagas have aristocratic, warlike heroes, the sagas of Icelanders describe characters who are essentially farmers or farmers' sons.
The sagas of Icelanders tell of the families who lived in Iceland from 930 to 1030.
The sagas of Icelanders were written down in Iceland mainly in the 13th century, and nothing is known of their authors.
Icelanders today can still read the old Icelandic sagas without difficulty.

title: The sagas' realism
description: The sagas of Icelanders stand out for realism and an objective style: their authors tried to show life in Iceland as it had really been, and Njals saga, often called the greatest, ends a farmer's hopeless struggle in fire.

facts.text: The sagas of Icelanders are known for realism, an objective style, tragic dignity and character portrayal.
Saga authors aimed at geographic, social and cultural truth to life, depicting Iceland as they had known it or imagined it had been.
Njals saga, often called the greatest saga, follows Njal, an influential farmer and sage, in a hopeless struggle that ends when his enemies burn his house with his family inside.

title: The Mahabharata's war
description: The Mahabharata, about seven times the Iliad and Odyssey combined, tells how two sets of cousins, the Kauravas and the Pandavas, fall out over a kingdom and fight a war at Kurukshetra.

facts.text: The Mahabharata has almost 100,000 couplets, about seven times the length of the Iliad and the Odyssey combined.
Tradition attributes the Mahabharata to the sage Vyasa; it grew over centuries and reached its present form about 400 CE.
The Mahabharata tells of a struggle for sovereignty between two groups of cousins, the Kauravas, sons of Dhritarashtra, and the Pandavas, sons of Pandu.
In a dice game set up by the Kaurava prince Duryodhana, the Pandavas lose their kingdom and are sent into the forest for 12 years.
The quarrel ends in a war at Kurukshetra in which all the Kauravas are killed.
The Mahabharata has been retold in written and oral Sanskrit and local-language versions throughout South and Southeast Asia.

title: The Bhagavad Gita in the Mahabharata
description: Inside the Mahabharata, on the brink of battle, Prince Arjuna balks at killing his own relatives; his charioteer Krishna counsels him, and their dialogue is the Bhagavad Gita, which Hindus revere.

facts.text: The Bhagavad Gita, part of Book VI of the Mahabharata, is a dialogue between Prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna, an avatar of the god Vishnu.
On the brink of battle, Arjuna is overwhelmed by misgivings about killing so many people, some of them his friends and relatives.
Krishna counsels Arjuna on his duty, and many Hindus have long cherished the Gita for spiritual guidance.

title: The Ramayana's story
description: Valmiki's Ramayana follows Prince Rama into 14 years of exile; the demon king Ravana carries off his wife Sita, and with the monkey general Hanuman, Rama defeats Ravana and rescues her.

facts.text: The Ramayana, a Sanskrit epic by the poet Valmiki, has about 24,000 couplets in seven books.
Rama, heir to the throne of Ayodhya, is exiled for 14 years with his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana.
In the forest, Ravana, the 10-headed demon king of Lanka, carries Sita off.
Rama embodies dharma (duty, honor and loyalty): the ideal son, husband and, in the end, king.
With the help of Hanuman, a devoted monkey general, Rama defeats Ravana and rescues Sita, a classic tale of good triumphing over evil.
In India, Ramlila ("Rama's play") stages the story during the nine-day Navratri festival, and Diwali marks Rama's return home from exile.

title: The Ramayana across Asia
description: The Ramayana spread in local forms across Southeast Asia, especially Cambodia, Indonesia and Thailand, where the Ramakien is the basis of khon dance-drama.

facts.text: The Ramayana spread in various forms throughout Southeast Asia, especially to Cambodia, Indonesia and Thailand.
Thailand's version is the Ramakien, and khon, Thailand's traditional dance-drama, is based on it.
Scenes from the Ramayana are carved in relief on Indonesian monuments, such as Panataran in eastern Java.

title: The epic of Sundiata
description: Sundiata Keita founded the Mali Empire in the 13th century; in the epic, the boy who could not walk stands up on an iron bar, survives exile and defeats Sumanguru at Kirina about 1235.

facts.text: Sundiata Keita, who died in 1255, founded the Mali Empire in West Africa.
In the epic, Sogolon's son Sundiata cannot walk as a child, and he and his mother are mocked at court.
In the epic, Sundiata finally pulls himself to his feet on a great iron bar, which bends into the shape of a bow.
Sumanguru, ruler of a neighboring state, overran Sundiata's homeland and killed his brothers, sparing Sundiata because he was a sickly boy.
Sundiata went into exile, then returned and decisively defeated Sumanguru at the Battle of Kirina about 1235.

title: Griots keep the epic alive
description: Griots (jeli), hereditary West African troubadour-historians, have kept Sundiata's story alive by performing it, many playing the 21-string kora; Niane's 1960 book is presented as a griot's telling.

facts.text: Sundiata's life is known from oral traditions repeated by griots, West Africa's storytellers.
Griots (jeli in the Mande languages) are hereditary West African troubadour-historians who preserve genealogies, historical narratives and oral traditions.
Many griots play the kora, a long-necked harp lute with 21 strings.
In 1960 Djibril Tamsir Niane published a French retelling of the epic, presented as told by the griot Djeli Mamadou Kouyate.

title: The trickster
description: A trickster is a story hero, often an animal, who is a bundle of opposites, creator and fool, and gets by on guile; Coyote and Raven are famous Native North American tricksters.

facts.text: A trickster is a hero, often an animal with human ways and magical powers, who is both creator and fool, destroyer and childish prankster.
Tricksters act by knavery, stupidity, gluttony or guile, most often a mix of these.
Coyote is possibly the most widely known Native North American trickster, and Raven plays the part among Northwest Coast peoples.

title: Ananse and Br'er Rabbit
description: Ananse, the Akan spider, won the sky god's stories by cunning and teaches through puzzles; Br'er Rabbit came from African folklore with enslaved Africans, published by Joel Chandler Harris in a criticized plantation frame.

facts.text: In one Akan story, the sky god Nyame sets Ananse three impossible tasks before making him King of All Wisdom Narratives: to capture a fierce big cat, hornets and a fairy.
Ananse completes the tasks by cunning rather than force.
Ananse, usually a spider, belongs to the Akan peoples, especially the Asante, and is famous across Africa, the Caribbean and beyond.
Ananse teaches values by leading people to the truth through puzzles, example and unexpected twists.
Br'er Rabbit is a trickster from African folklore, brought to the Americas by enslaved Africans.
Br'er Rabbit keeps outsmarting bigger animals like Br'er Fox and Br'er Bear: the small and weak beating the big and dull-witted.
Joel Chandler Harris, a white Atlanta journalist, heard the tales from enslaved people on a Georgia plantation and published them from 1880, told by Uncle Remus to a plantation owner's son.
The writer Alice Walker protested that Harris had stolen her African American folklore heritage and made it a white man's publishing commodity.

title: The Popol Vuh
description: The Popol Vuh, the K'iche' Maya 'Council Book', was written in K'iche' with the Latin alphabet between 1554 and 1558; the original is lost, and Francisco Ximenez's early-1700s copy survives in Chicago.

facts.text: The Popol Vuh, roughly "Council Book", was written by the K'iche' Maya between 1554 and 1558 in the K'iche' language, using the Latin alphabet.
The priest Francisco Ximenez found the manuscript in the early 1700s and copied it; the original is lost, and his copy is in the Newberry Library in Chicago.

title: People of maize
description: In the Popol Vuh, the K'iche' Maya tell how the gods, wanting beings who would remember them, made people of mud (dissolved), then of wood (heartless, turned to monkeys), and at last of maize.

facts.text: In the Popol Vuh, the gods want to make beings who will praise them and remember them.
The gods' first person, of mud, will not hold its shape and speaks nonsense, so they dissolve it.
The wooden people have no hearts and do not remember their makers; the gods send a great flood, and those who flee into the forest become monkeys.
The gods finally succeed, making human beings from maize.
The maize people see and know so much that the gods fear they will become as great as gods, so they cloud their sight, like breath on a mirror.

title: Shared roots
description: One explanation for similar myths is common origin: related peoples inherited them, as the cognate names of the sky gods Dyaus, Zeus and Jupiter show.

facts.text: The Vedic sky god Dyaus has a name cognate with those of Zeus of Greece and Jupiter ("Father Jove") of Rome; all three go back to the name of a Proto-Indo-European sky god.

title: Contact
description: A second explanation is contact: stories travel with the people who tell them, as with the Babylonian flood and Genesis, the Ramayana in Southeast Asia and Br'er Rabbit in the Americas.

facts.text: Stories travel with their tellers: the Ramayana spread through Southeast Asia, and Br'er Rabbit reached the Americas with enslaved Africans.

title: Shared human minds
description: A third explanation is shared minds: Adolf Bastian's psychic unity of humankind, with elementary ideas common to all peoples, which inspired Jung's collective unconscious.

facts.text: The ethnologist Adolf Bastian argued for a psychic unity of humankind: all peoples share certain elementary ideas, which take different forms in different environments.
Carl Jung's idea of a collective unconscious is believed to derive from Bastian's theory of elementary ideas.

title: Written down as the old world faded
description: Many of the chapter's myths were written down late, some at a turning point: Snorri explained the old myths for a Christian age, and the Popol Vuh was written when Maya beliefs were no longer tolerated.

facts.text: Snorri's Prose Edda was also meant to give a Christian age an understanding of the myths treated or alluded to in early poetry.
The Popol Vuh was written when the old beliefs of the Maya were no longer tolerated by their Christian conquerors, and its author says it is written because it can no longer be seen.

title: Freytag's pyramid
description: In 1863 Gustav Freytag pictured a drama as a pyramid: tension rises from the introduction to a climax, the turning point, then falls to the ending.

facts.text: Gustav Freytag published Die Technik des Dramas (The Technique of the Drama) in Leipzig in 1863.
Freytag described a drama as a pyramid of five parts: introduction, rise, climax, return or fall, and catastrophe.
The climax, from a Greek word for "ladder", is the turning point at which rising action turns into falling action.
In tragedy, the ending after the climax is often called the catastrophe.

title: The five parts of a plot
description: Exposition sets up, rising action complicates, the climax turns, falling action shows the consequences, and the resolution (denouement) unties the knot.

facts.text: Today the five parts are usually named exposition (setting, characters, background), rising action (complications that raise tension), climax, falling action (consequences) and resolution.
Denouement is French for "unknotting": the conclusion after the climax, where complications are unraveled and the conflict is resolved.

title: Conflict and its kinds
description: Conflict, a struggle between opposing forces, drives a plot. It is external (person vs person, nature or society) or internal (person vs self).

facts.text: A literary conflict is a struggle between two opposing forces, usually the main character and something else, and it drives the story forward.
Conflict can be external, against an outside force like another person, nature or society, or internal, inside a character's own mind.

Common kinds of conflict: person vs person (opposing goals), person vs nature, person vs society (its rules or traditions) and person vs self (an inner moral struggle); some lists add fate, the supernatural and technology.
In a conflict, opposing forces put obstacles between a character and what the character wants.

title: Flat and round characters
description: E. M. Forster's terms (1927): a flat character is built round a single idea or quality; a round one is complex and can surprise in a convincing way.

facts.text: Aspects of the Novel began as lectures E. M. Forster gave at Trinity College, Cambridge, in the spring of 1927, published the same year.
Forster wrote that flat characters, in their purest form, are "constructed round a single idea or quality" and can be summed up in one sentence.
Forster's example of a flat character is Mrs. Micawber in Dickens's David Copperfield, summed up by "I never will desert Mr. Micawber."
Forster said flat characters have advantages: they are easily recognized and easily remembered by the reader.
Round characters are complex and develop; Forster's test is "whether it is capable of surprising in a convincing way."

title: Character arcs
description: A dynamic character changes over a story (its arc), driven by the conflicts and plot; a static character does not. Scrooge is the classic case.

facts.text: A dynamic character goes through major inner change over a story, its character arc; a static character goes through little or none.
A dynamic character changes as a result of the story's conflicts and plot.
In Dickens's A Christmas Carol (1843), a miserly old man, Scrooge, is transformed into a kind benefactor after a series of ghosts visit him.

title: Point of view
description: The vantage point a story is told from: first person ("I"), third person limited (one character's mind) or omniscient (many minds). It sets what the reader can know.

facts.text: Point of view is the vantage point from which a story is presented.
In first-person narration the narrator says "I", is usually a character in the story, and gives only their own thoughts and feelings.
Third person limited tells the story from the standpoint of one character, who is not all-knowing, so the reader gets only that character's thoughts and actions.
Omniscient narration gives a panoramic view of the actions and inner feelings of the characters, and can move freely in time and place.
In Aspects of the Novel, Forster treats "the point of view from which the story may be told" as the novelist's second device, after kinds of character.

title: The unreliable narrator
description: A narrator who lies, leaves out or twists information, or misreads events; named by Wayne C. Booth (1961). Poe's Tell-Tale Heart is a classic case.

facts.text: An unreliable narrator tells lies, leaves out or misrepresents important information, or presents skewed readings of events as plain truth.
The critic Wayne C. Booth named the unreliable narrator in his 1961 book The Rhetoric of Fiction.
Some narrators are unreliable without meaning to be, through youth or inexperience; others have motives to mislead.
A narrator's unreliability shows as the reader learns more and new information contradicts what the narrator said.
Poe's "The Tell-Tale Heart" was published in The Pioneer in 1843; its narrator opens by asking "why will you say that I am mad?"
Poe's narrator offers as proof of sanity: "I heard all things in the heaven and in the earth. I heard many things in hell. How, then, am I mad?"
Poe's narrator says of the old man, "He had never wronged me," yet decides to take his life.
Poe's narrator is maddened by what he believes is the old man's loud heartbeat, still hears it after the murder, and hysterically confesses.

title: Theme
description: A story's theme is its central idea: take the subject (a word like "death") and add an assertion, in one sentence. A theme need not be a moral.

facts.text: A theme is the main or central idea of a literary work, its controlling insight, not a summary of its characters or events.
One way to state a theme: take the topic and add an assertion about it, in one sentence with a subject and a verb.
A moral is a recommendation for how to live; a theme does not have to be a moral, so ask what a story reveals, not what it teaches.
Britannica sees Gilgamesh's quest as reflecting the human struggle to come to terms with death, and says the epic suggests his legacy as ruler and builder will endure.

title: Symbols
description: A symbol is one thing, usually an object, that stands for something more abstract: the dove of peace, or the broken statue in Shelley's Ozymandias.

facts.text: In Genesis 8:11 (King James Version), the dove returns with "an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated from off the earth."
A symbol is one thing, usually a physical object, used to stand for something more abstract, by association or convention: the lion is a symbol of courage.
The dove is the bird portrayed and called the "dove of peace".
In Shelley's sonnet "Ozymandias" (1818), two vast, trunkless legs of stone stand in the desert; the pedestal says "Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!" and "Nothing beside remains."
Britannica reads the ruined statue in "Ozymandias" as showing a ruler's power vanquished by time.

title: Motifs
description: A motif is an element (object, image, sound, idea or word) that recurs through a work and points to its theme; a symbol can appear once, a motif must recur.

facts.text: A motif is an element, such as an object, image, sound, idea or word, that recurs through a work and points toward its theme.
A motif must recur through a story, while a symbol can appear just once.

title: The hero's journey
description: Joseph Campbell's monomyth (1949): a hero leaves the everyday world, is tested, wins a boon and returns. Separation, initiation, return; 17 stages.

facts.text: Joseph Campbell's The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) argued that the world's myths share one basic story, which he called the monomyth.
The monomyth's core is separation, initiation and return: the hero sets out, has transformative adventures and comes home, bringing back a boon.
George Lucas drew on The Hero with a Thousand Faces for Star Wars.
Campbell lays out 17 stages: Departure (5, from the Call to Adventure to the Belly of the Whale), Initiation (6, the Road of Trials to the Ultimate Boon) and Return (6, ending with Freedom to Live).
Early stages include the Call to Adventure, Refusal of the Call, Supernatural Aid and the Crossing of the First Threshold.
Critics argue that Campbell's links between myths rest on his own subjective interpretation.

title: Genre and its promises
description: A genre (French, "kind") is a category of literary work with recurring conventions and audience expectations; writers can keep those promises or cleverly break them.

facts.text: Genre, from a French word for "kind", is a distinctive type or category of literary work, such as the epic, tragedy, comedy, novel and short story.
Genres are recognized by recurring conventions, purposes and audience expectations.
Audiences expect a genre's expectations to be satisfied, and writers can either follow its conventions or manipulate them.
In Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey (published 1817), Catherine Morland is introduced to Gothic novels like Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho.
At the abbey Catherine finds a mysterious roll of old papers, and by daylight sees she "held a washing-bill in her hand."
Northanger Abbey is a satire that subverts the popular plot devices of Gothic fiction: haunted castles, the supernatural, a central mystery and suspense.
Catherine becomes convinced that General Tilney murdered his wife, until his son Henry firmly sets her straight.

title: Story versus plot
description: Forster: "The king died and then the queen died" is a story, events in time order; add "of grief" and it is a plot, with the emphasis on cause.

facts.text: Forster: "The king died and then the queen died" is a story, events in time sequence; "The king died, and then the queen died of grief" is a plot, stressing causality.

title: The poetic line
description: Poetry depends on the line more than prose does; lines can be end-stopped or enjambed, and a line break can slow a reader down.

facts.text: In his Table Talk entry of July 12, 1827, Samuel Taylor Coleridge called prose "words in their best order" and poetry "the best words in the best order".
Formally, poetry is recognizable by its greater dependence than prose on the line.
Enjambment is the continuation of a sentence or clause across a line break, from the French enjamber, "to stride over"; an end-stopped line ends with punctuation.
William Carlos Williams's "The Red Wheelbarrow", first published in Spring and All in 1923, splits "wheelbarrow" across a line break: "a red wheel / barrow".
By breaking "wheelbarrow" into "wheel" and "barrow" across a line, Williams slows the reading and fixes the image in the reader's mind.

title: Compression and sound
description: Poetry concentrates experience in language chosen for meaning, sound and rhythm, and it is older than literacy.

facts.text: Poetry is literature that evokes a concentrated imaginative awareness of experience through language chosen and arranged for its meaning, sound and rhythm.
Poetry predates literacy and precedes prose in all literatures.

title: Meter and feet
description: Meter measures the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in feet; an iamb rises (today), a trochee falls (matter).

facts.text: An iamb is a foot of two syllables, unstressed then stressed, as in "today"; a trochee is the reverse, stressed then unstressed, as in "matter".
Meter, from the Greek metron ("measure"), is the measured pattern of rhythmic accents in a line of verse, counted in feet of stressed and unstressed syllables.
Line lengths are named with Greek prefixes: tetrameter has four feet, pentameter five and hexameter six.
Poems in trochaic meter include Edgar Allan Poe's "The Raven" and works by William Blake.

title: Iambic pentameter and blank verse
description: Five iambs make a line of iambic pentameter, the line of Shakespeare's plays and sonnets; unrhymed, it is blank verse.

facts.text: Iambic pentameter is a line of five iambic feet, about ten syllables alternating unstressed and stressed.
Shakespeare famously wrote his plays and sonnets in iambic pentameter; Sonnet 73's "That time of year thou mayst in me behold" is an example.
Blank verse is unrhymed verse in a regular meter, usually iambic pentameter; it was the standard line for Shakespeare and Milton.

title: Rhyme and slant rhyme
description: Rhyme matches sounds, usually at line ends; perfect rhyme matches fully (bright, flight), slant rhyme only nearly (young, long).

facts.text: Rhyme is the correspondence of sounds; in a perfect rhyme the final stressed vowel and all following sounds match (bright, flight), while a slant rhyme only nearly matches (young, long).
Ancient Greek and Roman poets rarely if ever rhymed; rhyme took hold in Western poetry in the Middle Ages, while China's earliest surviving rhymes date to about the 10th century BCE.

title: Alliteration and assonance
description: Alliteration repeats consonant sounds, usually at word beginnings; assonance repeats vowel sounds in nearby words.

facts.text: Shakespeare's Sonnet 30 opens: "When to the sessions of sweet silent thought / I summon up remembrance of things past", an example of alliteration.
Alliteration is the repetition of consonant sounds, especially at the beginnings of nearby words; its pleasing, memorable sounds make it common in nursery rhymes and advertising.
Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words; the word comes from the Latin assonare, "to answer with the same sound".

title: Simile and metaphor
description: Both compare unlike things; a simile says so with like or as, while a metaphor speaks as if one thing is the other.

facts.text: Robert Burns's song "A Red, Red Rose" opens: "O my Luve's like a red, red rose, / That's newly sprung in June".
A simile compares two unlike things and makes the resemblance explicit with "like" or "as".
A metaphor compares unlike things without "like" or "as", applying a description to something it does not literally fit: "my love is like a flower" is a simile, "my love is a flower" a metaphor.
Metaphor comes from the Greek metaphora, "a transfer", a carrying over.
In Shakespeare's As You Like It, Jaques says: "All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players; / They have their exits and their entrances".

title: Imagery
description: Imagery is language that calls up the senses; simile and metaphor are two ways to build it.

facts.text: Imagery is language representing sensory experience (sight, sound, smell, touch and taste); simile and metaphor can create it, building an experience for readers to imagine.

title: The sonnet and its two forms
description: A sonnet is 14 lines, traditionally iambic pentameter; the Italian form splits 8 and 6 lines, the English form three quatrains and a couplet.

facts.text: Shakespeare's Sonnet 130 opens: "My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun; / Coral is far more red, than her lips red".
In Sonnet 130 the first twelve lines compare the speaker's mistress unfavorably with the usual beauties of nature, and the closing couplet swerves in a surprising direction.
A sonnet is a 14-line poem, traditionally in iambic pentameter with a set rhyme scheme; the name comes from the Italian sonetto, "a little sound or song".
The sonnet began among Sicilian court poets in the 13th century; Petrarch perfected the Italian form, and Sir Thomas Wyatt and Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, brought it to England in the 16th century.
The Petrarchan or Italian sonnet has an octave of eight lines (abbaabba) followed by an answering sestet of six.
The Shakespearean or English sonnet has three quatrains and a couplet, rhyming abab cdcd efef gg.

title: The volta
description: A sonnet turns: between lines 8 and 9 in the Italian form, before the final couplet in the English form.

facts.text: The volta, Italian for "turn", is the shift in a poem's thought, often marked by "but" or "yet"; it comes between lines 8 and 9 of a Petrarchan sonnet and before the final couplet of a Shakespearean one.
Sonnet 130 ends: "And yet by heaven, I think my love as rare, / As any she belied with false compare": she is as lovely as any woman praised with false comparisons.

title: Haiku
description: A haiku is 17 syllables in lines of 5, 7 and 5, grown from the hokku that opened a renga; it catches one brief moment.

facts.text: A traditional haiku has 17 syllables in three lines of 5, 7 and 5.
Haiku grew from the hokku, the opening stanza of a renga, a long linked poem often written by several poets taking turns.
In the 17th century Matsuo Basho raised the hokku into a refined art of its own.
Haiku focuses on a brief moment in time and can be read in one breath.

title: Basho's old pond
description: Basho's 1686 frog poem: a cutting word splits stillness from splash, and the frog marks spring.

facts.text: According to his disciple Shiko, Basho composed the frog poem on a spring day in 1686, hearing frogs jump into his garden pond, and found its last two lines before its opening.
Basho's poem reads furuike ya / kawazu tobikomu / mizu no oto: the old pond, a frog jumps in, the sound of water.
In the frog poem, ya is a cutting word (kireji) that separates and yet joins the phrases before and after it.
In Japanese poetry the frog is a season word (kigo) for spring.
Classical poems gave the frog a plaintive singing voice; Basho instead gave the sound of a frog jumping into water.

title: Free verse
description: Free verse drops regular meter and rhyme and follows the cadences of speech, but it keeps the line.

facts.text: Ezra Pound urged poets "to compose in the sequence of the musical phrase, not in sequence of a metronome" (A Retrospect, 1918).
Free verse is poetry without a regular meter or set form, organized instead to the cadences of speech.
The term free verse translates the French vers libre, the name of a movement that began in France in the 1880s.
Free verse keeps a visual form and uses the line to set itself apart from prose.
A great ancestor of free verse is the King James Bible's Psalms and Song of Songs, whose parallelism and repetitions, following Hebrew cadences, inspired poets from Blake to Whitman.

title: Rhythm without meter
description: Free verse builds rhythm by patterning sounds, words, phrases and sentences, as in Whitman's repetitions.

facts.text: Free verse rhythms are based on patterned elements such as sounds, words, phrases and sentences rather than traditional metrical units.
Walt Whitman is regarded as the founding father (progenitor) of American free verse.
Whitman's Song of Myself opens: "I celebrate myself, and sing myself, / And what I assume you shall assume".

title: How epics open
description: Epics call on the Muse (invocation) and plunge in medias res, into the middle of things.

facts.text: In his Ars Poetica, Horace praised Homer for not starting the Trojan War ab ovo, "from the egg" (the egg from which Helen was born), but hurrying the listener in medias res.
A common epic convention is the invocation, in which the poet appeals to a Muse or god for inspiration at or near the start.
In Samuel Butler's translations, the Iliad opens "Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus" and the Odyssey "Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero".
John Milton's Paradise Lost keeps the convention, calling in its opening lines: "Sing, Heavenly Muse".
Epics often begin in medias res ("into the middle of things"), plunging into a crucial situation in a chain of events.
The Iliad does not recount the whole Trojan War: it covers a few crucial weeks in the war's final year and focuses on the wrath of Achilles.

title: The epic simile
description: An epic (Homeric) simile stretches a comparison over several lines to raise the heroic scene.

facts.text: An epic simile is an extended simile running to several lines, used in epic poetry to intensify the heroic stature of its subject and as decoration.
In Butler's Iliad (Book VII): "As when the rising west wind furs the face of the sea and the waters grow dark beneath it, so sat the companies of Trojans and Achaeans upon the plain."

title: Aristotle's tragic hero and catharsis
description: Aristotle's tragic hero falls through an error (hamartia), and tragedy works through pity and fear toward catharsis.

facts.text: In S. H. Butcher's translation of the Poetics, the tragic hero is not eminently good, is "highly renowned and prosperous", and falls "not by vice or depravity, but by some error or frailty".
Aristotle's word hamartia comes from the Greek hamartanein, "to err"; he meant an error of judgment, though later critics read it as a moral flaw such as jealousy.
In the Oedipus story, Oedipus unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother.
Butcher's Poetics defines tragedy as an imitation of a serious action that, "through pity and fear", effects "the proper purgation of these emotions".
Catharsis is Greek for purgation or purification; no single interpretation of Aristotle's meaning, purging feelings or a cleansing more like ritual, has won general agreement.

title: Reversal and recognition
description: Aristotle's peripeteia (reversal) turns the action to its opposite; anagnorisis (recognition) moves from ignorance to knowledge, best when they coincide.

facts.text: In Aristotle's example from Oedipus, the messenger comes to cheer Oedipus and free him from his fears about his mother, but by revealing who he is produces the opposite effect.
Aristotle's peripeteia, the Reversal of the Situation, is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite.
Aristotle's anagnorisis, Recognition, is a change from ignorance to knowledge; the best recognition comes together with a reversal, as in Oedipus.

title: Reading The Tyger with the poet's toolkit
description: Blake's The Tyger (1794) shows meter, rhyme, alliteration, imagery and a one-word turn working together.

facts.text: Blake's The Tyger appeared in Songs of Innocence and of Experience (1794) and opens: "Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night".
Critics describe The Tyger's meter as mostly trochaic: four beats a line that start on a stressed syllable, as in "Tyger Tyger, burning bright".
The first stanza ends "What immortal hand or eye, / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?", with alliteration in "frame" and "fearful".
The Tyger likens the making of the tiger to fashioning molten metal from a furnace with hammer and anvil: "What the hammer? what the chain, / In what furnace was thy brain?"
The Tyger is a series of questions that are never fully answered, including "Did he who made the Lamb make thee?"
The Tyger's last stanza repeats the first, except that "Could frame thy fearful symmetry?" becomes "Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?"

title: Antigone: conscience against law
description: Sophocles' Antigone sets a sister's duty to bury her brother against King Creon's edict; Creon's rigid law defies the gods and destroys his family.

facts.text: In Sophocles' Antigone, Creon, king of Thebes, forbids the burial of Polyneices, who attacked the city, and Antigone, his sister, buries him anyway.
Some evidence suggests that Antigone was first performed in 442 or 441 BCE.
Antigone's conflict sets the valid claims of conscience (her duty to give her brother a proper burial) against law (Creon's edict that enemies of the state not be buried).
Creon's rigid adherence to state law makes him defy the gods by denying humanity's common obligations toward the dead.
By the time the prophet Tiresias persuades Creon to relent, Antigone has killed herself; Creon's son Haemon and then his wife Eurydice also kill themselves.

title: Why Antigone is still staged
description: Antigone's clash of law and conscience fits any age of defiance, as Jean Anouilh's version in occupied Paris (1944) showed.

facts.text: Jean Anouilh's Antigone, a French play based on Sophocles' tragedy, was first performed in Paris on 6 February 1944, during the Nazi occupation.

title: The Tang golden age of poetry
description: The Tang dynasty (618 to 907) is called the golden age of Chinese poetry: nearly 49,000 poems survive, officials were hired through literary exams, and regulated verse set strict rules.

facts.text: Under the Tang dynasty (618 to 907), often called the golden age of Chinese literature, poetry was the greatest glory of the period.
More than 48,900 poems by more than 2,200 Tang poets have been preserved.
The Tang expanded the use of examinations in literature and culture for hiring civil servants.
A popular Tang form, lüshi or regulated verse, had eight lines of five or seven syllables set to strict tonal patterns.

title: Li Bai and Du Fu
description: Li Bai, the romantic free spirit of wine and the Moon, and Du Fu, master of regulated verse and poet of compassion in wartime, are the two giants of Tang poetry.

facts.text: Li Bai (701 to 762), a romantic, celebrated drinking, friendship, solitude and nature, and avoided the strict lüshi for freer forms.
Popular tradition says Li Bai drowned when, sitting drunk in a boat, he tried to seize the Moon's reflection in the water.
Du Fu received a traditional Confucian education but failed the imperial examinations of 735.
Du Fu (712 to 770), whom many critics consider China's greatest poet, lived through poverty and exile after An Lushan's rebellion of 755 and wrote with compassion for people caught in war.
Du Fu refined the lüshi, or regulated verse, to a point of glowing intensity.

title: Journey to the West
description: A Ming novel of 100 chapters that turns the monk Xuanzang's real pilgrimage to India into 81 adventures with invented companions, full of comedy and satire.

facts.text: Journey to the West is based on the real 7th-century pilgrimage of the Buddhist monk Xuanzang (602 to 664) to India in search of sacred texts.
Journey to the West, a 100-chapter novel of China's Ming dynasty, is usually credited to Wu Cheng'en.
In the novel the monk, called Tripitaka, travels with three animal spirits, the magically gifted Monkey, the clumsy Pigsy and the fish spirit Sandy, through 81 adventures.
Beyond its adventures, Journey to the West offers biting satire of society and Chinese bureaucracy, and it can be read as an allegory.
Arthur Waley's abridged English translation of Journey to the West, titled Monkey, appeared in 1942.

title: Sun Wukong, the Monkey King
description: Born from a stone egg, Monkey defies heaven, is imprisoned under a mountain by the Buddha, then is freed to protect the pilgrim monk.

facts.text: Journey to the West begins with the birth of a monkey, Sun Wukong, from a stone egg; he gains magic powers such as shape-shifting and somersaulting through clouds.
After challenging the Jade Emperor's authority, Monkey is subdued by the Buddha and imprisoned beneath the Five Elements Mountain.
Released through the bodhisattva Guanyin, Monkey agrees to protect the monk on his journey, and by the end of the novel he attains Buddhahood.

title: The Tale of Genji as a novel
description: Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji (about 1010) follows one courtier and his legacy through 54 chapters with deep feeling, which is why it is often called the first novel.

facts.text: Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji while she was a lady in attendance at the Japanese court.
The Tale of Genji sustains its story through 54 chapters of one character and his legacy.
The hero, Genji, is a handsome, sensitive, gifted courtier, an excellent lover and a worthy friend.
The Tale of Genji shows supreme sensitivity to human emotions and nature, and its darkening tone reflects the Buddhist conviction of this world's transience.
The Tale of Genji is an absorbing introduction to the culture of the aristocracy in early Heian Japan: its entertainment, dress, daily life and moral code.

title: Murasaki Shikibu and the women writers of Heian Japan
description: At the Heian court men wrote official Chinese; hiragana gave women their chance to write literature. Murasaki, whose real name is unknown, also learned Chinese.

facts.text: Murasaki Shikibu's real name is unknown.
Murasaki Shikibu learned Chinese, then generally the exclusive sphere of males.
At the Heian court, men composed official documents in stilted Chinese, and the hiragana script gave court women an opportunity to create works of literature.

title: Scheherazade's frame story
description: In the Nights, Scheherazade saves her life by leaving each story unfinished; that outer story is a frame that holds all the other tales.

facts.text: In the Nights' frame story, King Shahryar, after discovering his wife's infidelity, marries and kills a new wife each day.
Shahrazad (Scheherazade) tells the king a story each evening, leaving it incomplete; he puts off her execution day after day and finally abandons his cruel plan.
A frame story is an overall unifying story within which one or more tales are related.

title: How the Nights kept growing
description: The Nights gathered stories from many lands and kept growing in translation: Aladdin and Ali Baba reached it through Galland and the Aleppo storyteller Hanna Diyab.

facts.text: The Nights draws on stories from India, Iran, Iraq, Egypt, Turkey and possibly Greece; its Persian source was the Hazār afsāna, "A Thousand Tales".
Antoine Galland's French translation, published from 1704 to 1717, was the first European edition of the Nights.
The tales of the Nights best known in the West, such as Aladdin and Ali Baba, were later additions to the original collection.
Hanna Diyab, a young Syrian from Aleppo, told Antoine Galland stories in Paris in 1709, including Aladdin, and they fed the last volumes of his Nights.

title: Ferdowsi's Shahnameh
description: The Shahnameh (Book of Kings), finished in 1010, is the Persian national epic, running from Iran's mythical kings to the Arab conquest; its best-known tragedy is Rostam and Sohrab.

facts.text: Ferdowsi gave the Persian national epic, the Shahnameh ("Book of Kings"), its final form; completed in 1010, it runs from mythical times to the Arab conquest of the 7th century.
The Shahnameh is a mixture of myth, legend and history.
The Shahnameh's legendary first section includes its most famous story, the tragic fight between Rostam and his son Sohrab, which ends with the father unwittingly killing his son.

title: The Shahnameh and the Persian language
description: Written in nearly pure Persian when Arabic dominated writing, the Shahnameh became Iranians' literary expression of their nation, and it is credited with keeping Persian alive.

facts.text: Persian was the first language in Muslim civilization to break through Arabic's monopoly on writing, emerging again as a written language in the 9th century.
Based on a Pahlavi (Middle Persian) original, the Shahnameh's language is pure Persian with only the slightest admixture of Arabic.
The Shahnameh quickly became of great importance to Iranians as the literary expression of their national sentiments.

title: Beowulf, the Old English epic
description: Beowulf, set in 6th-century Scandinavia, fights Grendel, Grendel's mother and at last a dragon; it is the highest achievement of Old English literature.

facts.text: Beowulf fights the monster Grendel at King Hrothgar's hall Heorot, then Grendel's mother; after ruling in peace for 50 years, he dies fighting a fire-breathing dragon.
Beowulf takes place in early 6th-century Scandinavia, mainly in what are now Denmark and Sweden.
The date of Beowulf's composition is uncertain; some scholars believe it was written in the 8th century.
Beowulf is the highest achievement of Old English literature and the earliest European vernacular epic.

title: The single Beowulf manuscript
description: Beowulf survives in one manuscript, made around 1000, which came through a fire in 1731 with much of its text still readable.

facts.text: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, Cotton MS Vitellius A XV, made around the year 1000.
The Beowulf manuscript was damaged by fire in 1731, but much of its text remains readable.

title: Dante's journey through the afterlife
description: The Divine Comedy (about 1308 to 1321) takes Dante through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise in 100 cantos, guided by Virgil and then Beatrice.

facts.text: The Divine Comedy, written in Italian from about 1308 to 1321, has 100 cantos in three sections: Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso.
The Roman poet Virgil guides Dante until the summit of Purgatory, where Beatrice takes over and guides him through Paradise.
The Divine Comedy's rhyme scheme is terza rima, an Italian verse form of three-line stanzas.
In Longfellow's translation, the Inferno opens: "Midway upon the journey of our life / I found myself within a forest dark, / For the straightforward pathway had been lost."

title: Dante chooses Italian
description: Dante wrote in Italian rather than Latin to reach a wider audience and give a voice to lay culture, a choice with a revolutionary impact on the Italian language.

facts.text: By choosing to write his poem in the Italian vernacular rather than in Latin, Dante decisively influenced the course of literary development.
Dante's use of the vernacular ensured that his writing would reach a wider audience.
In writing in Italian, Dante lent a voice to the emerging lay culture of his own country.
Dante's choice to write in Italian rather than Latin had a revolutionary impact on the development of the Italian language and on Western literature.

title: The Canterbury Tales' pilgrimage frame
description: Chaucer's pilgrims tell tales in a contest on the road to Canterbury; the frame lets people from across society tell every kind of story.

facts.text: In The Canterbury Tales (written 1387 to 1400), about 30 pilgrims gather at the Tabard Inn in Southwark to visit Becket's shrine at Canterbury, and the Host proposes a storytelling contest with a free supper for the best tale.
Chaucer left The Canterbury Tales unfinished at his death, with 24 tales completed.
In The Canterbury Tales, the pilgrimage frame brings together varied tellers of tales, who emerge as vivid personalities.
The pilgrims range from a knight to a miller, the Wife of Bath and a pardoner, and their tales span courtly romance, fabliau, saint's life and beast fable.
Having the pilgrims, rather than Chaucer himself, tell the tales gave him an unprecedented freedom to explore many genres.
John Dryden wrote of Chaucer's pilgrims: "'Tis sufficient to say, according to the proverb, that here is God's plenty."

title: Chaucer chooses English
description: While a fellow poet like Gower wrote weighty works in French and Latin, Chaucer, fluent in French, wrote in English and was hailed as "the first finder of our language".

facts.text: Chaucer's contemporary John Gower wrote two of his weighty works in French and Latin.
Chaucer was doubtless as fluent in French as in the Middle English of his time.
Chaucer's decision to write in English is not easy to account for; his earliest substantial poems were heavily indebted to fashionable French courtly love poetry.
Chaucer, the outstanding English poet before Shakespeare, has been called "the first finder of our language."

title: Why some stories last
description: Old stories last when a copy is kept (often by luck), when they carry a language, and when later ages retell and translate them.

facts.text: Arthur Waley's English translation of The Tale of Genji appeared from 1925 to 1933.

title: The Globe and its crowd
description: Shakespeare's company opened the open-air Globe on Bankside in 1599; a penny bought a standing place among the groundlings, and every class came.

facts.text: Shakespeare's company opened the Globe on London's Bankside in 1599, built from the timbers of their old playhouse, the Theatre.
The Globe was an open-air playhouse: the yard around the stage had only the sky for a roof.
At the Globe a penny bought a standing place among the groundlings in the yard; another penny bought a gallery bench, and the Lords' Rooms cost most.
Playhouses like the Globe held audiences of two or three thousand, squeezed tightly together.
Playgoers came from nearly every class: a visitor in 1617 saw porters and carters round the stage, apprentices spent spare time there, and wealthier people and royalty came too.
Audiences came from every class, and Shakespeare wrote for them all.
Shakespeare's stages had little or no scenery, so playwrights used dialogue and hand props to tell the audience where the action was.
In Hamlet, the prince mocks actors who overact "to split the ears of the groundlings", the cheapest-paying playgoers standing in the yard.

title: Clowns in the tragedies
description: To hold a crowd from every class, Shakespeare put clowns in his tragedies and kings in his comedies.

facts.text: Shakespeare put clowns in his tragedies and kings in his comedies.
Some of Shakespeare's most popular clowns appear in his greatest tragedies, such as the gravediggers in Hamlet and the Porter in Macbeth.

title: Hamlet's hidden mind
description: Hamlet hides his thoughts from the court behind a show of madness; only his soliloquies show the audience what he thinks and plans.

facts.text: Early in Hamlet, the prince tells the court he has "that within which passeth show".
In Hamlet, written about 1599 to 1601, the ghost of Hamlet's father says Claudius poisoned him, and Claudius has married Hamlet's mother, Gertrude, and become king.
Hamlet puts "an antic disposition" on, a show of madness, to deceive Claudius and the court.
Alone at the end of Act 2, Hamlet fears the ghost may be the devil and plans a play: "The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the King."
In Act 3, Hamlet's soliloquy "To be, or not to be" weighs whether it is nobler to suffer life's troubles or to fight them; it is Shakespeare's most famous soliloquy.

title: The soliloquy
description: A soliloquy is a character's thoughts spoken aloud while alone on stage (Latin solus, alone, and loqui, to speak); an aside is a brief remark only the audience hears.

facts.text: A soliloquy is a passage in a play in which a character speaks their thoughts or feelings aloud while alone on stage or while the other actors keep silent.
The word soliloquy comes from Latin solus, "alone", and loqui, "to speak".
An aside is a brief remark the audience hears but the other characters on stage supposedly do not.

title: Shakespeare's borrowed plots
description: Playwrights of Shakespeare's time happily reworked old stories; Romeo and Juliet came from Arthur Brooke's popular 1562 poem, with Ovid's Pyramus and Thisbe behind it.

facts.text: Romeo and Juliet opens with a Prologue announcing that "A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life".
Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet about 1594 to 1596; his main source was Arthur Brooke's poem The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet (1562), from a French version of a Bandello tale.
Playwrights of Shakespeare's time were not too bothered about being original; they reworked old stories and even used other people's plots.
With a few exceptions, Shakespeare did not invent the plots of his plays.

title: What Shakespeare added to Romeo and Juliet
description: Shakespeare squeezed Brooke's nine months into four days, grew Mercutio from a walk-on guest, and dropped Brooke's warning to disobedient youth.

facts.text: Shakespeare compressed a story that takes at least nine months in Brooke's poem into four days, Sunday to Thursday morning.
In Brooke's poem Mercutio is only a guest at Capulet's feast; his Queen Mab speech, his jokes and his death are Shakespeare's inventions.
Brooke's preface condemns the lovers as a warning against neglecting parents' authority; Shakespeare does not follow his lead.

title: Disguise and weddings in the comedies
description: In Twelfth Night and As You Like It, a heroine disguised as a young man tangles the plot until the truth comes out and the comedy ends in weddings.

facts.text: In Shakespeare's England, women's roles were played by boys.
On Shakespeare's stage, Viola in Twelfth Night was a boy playing a girl playing a boy for most of the play.
In Twelfth Night (about 1600 to 1602), shipwrecked Viola, thinking her twin Sebastian drowned, disguises herself as a young man, Cesario, and serves Duke Orsino.
Orsino sends Cesario to woo Countess Olivia for him, and Olivia falls in love with the messenger.
Caught in the tangle, Viola says: "O time, thou must untangle this, not I".
In As You Like It (about 1598 to 1600), Rosalind, disguised as a young man called Ganymede, gets lovesick Orlando to woo her as if she were Rosalind.
In Twelfth Night, Sebastian's return causes mistaken identity until the twins' identities are revealed and the lovers pair off.
Shakespeare's comedies, despite bickering and mistaken identity, frequently end with the promise of a wedding, sometimes several.

title: Dramatic irony
description: Dramatic irony is when the audience understands more than the characters do; disguise plots run on it.

facts.text: Dramatic irony is a device in which the audience's understanding of events or people surpasses the characters', giving their words a double meaning.

title: Words and phrases from Shakespeare
description: Shakespeare's works give the first recorded use of many words and phrases, like the green-eyed monster, some made by turning nouns into verbs; some have shifted meaning since.

facts.text: In Othello, Iago warns: "beware, my lord, of jealousy; / It is the green-ey'd monster"; jealousy is still called the green-eyed monster.
Shakespeare's works give the first recorded use of a great many English words; he may have made many by combining words, turning nouns into verbs or adding prefixes and suffixes.
Shakespeare was the first writer on record to use partner, property and scissor as verbs, though he did not invent the words.
In Romeo and Juliet, Mercutio's "wild-goose chase" was a horse race in which the leader chose any course and the others had to follow; today it means a fruitless search.

title: What "first recorded" means
description: A word first recorded in Shakespeare is the earliest written use found so far, not proof he invented it; dictionary readers combed his works hardest, and earlier uses keep turning up.

facts.text: A word's earliest known use means the earliest evidence found so far, not that the word was invented then.
The Oxford English Dictionary's original editors and hundreds of volunteer readers recorded Shakespeare's language in more detail than any other writer's.
Assassination, used in Macbeth, appears earlier in a 1572 letter by the diplomat Sir Thomas Smith.

title: Don Quixote and Sancho Panza
description: Cervantes's two-part novel (1605, 1615) parodies chivalric romances: a gentleman crazed by them rides out as a knight with the proverb-loving peasant Sancho Panza.

facts.text: In Don Quixote, an aging gentleman so enamoured of chivalric romances that he loses his wits sets out as a wandering knight, with the peasant Sancho Panza as his squire.
Miguel de Cervantes published Don Quixote in two parts, in 1605 and 1615; it began as a parody of the chivalric romances then in vogue.
Don Quixote mistakes a row of windmills for giants and charges them.
Sancho Panza is a short, earthy peasant famous for his proverbs, whose common sense is a foil to his master's idealism; Cervantes built much of the story on their relationship.

title: Why Don Quixote is called the first modern novel
description: Don Quixote sets many voices and points of view against each other and, in Part 2, lets characters who have read Part 1 meet its hero; it is often called the first modern novel.

facts.text: Don Quixote is considered a prototype of the modern novel, with many characters of diverse beliefs and perspectives: the multiple voices modern fiction depends on.
In Part 2 of Don Quixote, characters have already read Part 1 and know about its hero; some use it to play tricks on him.
A spurious sequel by one Avellaneda appeared in 1614, and Cervantes answered it in his own Part 2.

title: Robinson Crusoe and the new realism
description: Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719) passed itself off as a castaway's true memoir, told in plain, concrete detail about one ordinary man.

facts.text: The word novel is a shortened form of the Italian novella, from Latin novus, meaning "new".
Daniel Defoe was 59 when he published his first novel, Robinson Crusoe, in 1719.
Robinson Crusoe first appeared as the Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, "Written by Himself", presenting the story as Crusoe's own account.
Defoe's novels are known for their plain, matter-of-fact style and vivid concreteness of detail.
Crusoe builds a raft to strip the wreck of food, tools and sailcloth, and learns to grow corn, barley and rice.

title: The readers behind the novel's rise
description: From about 1650, more reading matter spread education to the middle classes, especially women; lending libraries and hits like Pamela (1740) made 18th-century Britain a novel-reading nation.

facts.text: The growth in reading matter after about 1650 spread education to the middle classes, especially women, and this wider readership shows in the rich 18th-century growth of the prose novel.
In the 18th century, especially in England, circulating and subscription libraries were in vogue and shaped popular literary taste, especially in fiction.
Samuel Richardson's Pamela (1740), a novel in letters about a servant woman who resists her employer and is rewarded with marriage, was a publishing sensation.
Pamela provoked parodies, among them Henry Fielding's Shamela (1741).

title: Gulliver's Travels
description: Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726) sends its hero to tiny Lilliput, giant Brobdingnag, flying Laputa and the land of the rational horses, the Houyhnhnms.

facts.text: In Lilliput, Gulliver hears that "eleven thousand persons" have died rather than obey a law to break their eggs at the smaller end.
Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels appeared anonymously in 1726; Gulliver visits Lilliput, the giants of Brobdingnag, the flying island of Laputa, and the Houyhnhnms.
In the last voyage, rational horses, the Houyhnhnms, rule over brutish humanlike creatures, the Yahoos.
The Lilliputians are less than 6 inches tall, and their tiny size mirrors their small-mindedness.

title: Satire
description: Satire holds vices and follies up to ridicule, exaggerating them until the familiar looks absurd; Swift's egg war and heel parties shrink real quarrels to size.

facts.text: Lilliput's war over which end of an egg to break mocks religious quarrels, and its parties, split by high or low heels, stand for England's Tories and Whigs.
Satire is an art form in which vices, follies and abuses are held up to censure by ridicule, irony, parody, caricature or other methods.
The satirist exaggerates objectionable features to create a distorted image, so readers see the absurdity in the familiar.
After Gulliver praises England, Brobdingnag's king calls its people "the most pernicious race of little odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon the surface of the earth".

title: Austen's irony
description: Pride and Prejudice (1813) opens with a grave universal truth that turns out to describe families hunting rich husbands for their daughters: Austen trusts readers to catch the irony.

facts.text: Pride and Prejudice opens: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife."
The next sentence says the neighborhood families consider such a man "the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters".
Pride and Prejudice was published anonymously in 1813.
Readers have long enjoyed the opening's ironic contrasts: between what it seems to say and the marriage market it describes, and between its grave tone and comic drop.

title: Free indirect discourse
description: Austen made pioneering use of free indirect discourse, third-person narration that takes on a character's voice without "he thought", letting readers hear a mind and its blind spots.

facts.text: Free indirect discourse is third-person narration that keeps some elements of a first-person voice, giving a character's thoughts without "he thought"; Austen was one of the first to use it.
In Persuasion, the narration takes on Captain Wentworth's view of Anne Elliot, who once gave him up: "He had not forgiven Anne Elliot. She had used him ill, deserted and disappointed him."
Austen uses free indirect speech to comically undercut a heroine, letting readers see her mistakes from inside her own thoughts.
Austen first gave the novel its distinctly modern character through her treatment of ordinary people in everyday life.

title: The First Folio
description: Seven years after Shakespeare died, his fellow actors Heminges and Condell published 36 of his plays in the First Folio (1623); 18 had never been printed and might otherwise be lost.

facts.text: In 1623 Shakespeare's fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell, partners in the King's Men, published 36 of his plays as the First Folio.
The First Folio appeared in 1623, seven years after Shakespeare's death in 1616.
Of the First Folio's 36 plays, 18, including Macbeth, The Tempest, As You Like It and Twelfth Night, had never been printed before; without it, half of Shakespeare's plays might have been lost.

title: Lyrical Ballads and the Preface
description: Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads (1798) is seen as the start of English Romanticism: poems of common life in the language really used by men, driven by powerful feeling.

facts.text: In 1798 William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge published Lyrical Ballads, a slim volume with no author's name on it.
Lyrical Ballads is widely regarded as the beginning of the English Romantic movement.
The poems of Lyrical Ballads set out to break the decorum of Neoclassical verse.
Wordsworth's Preface to Lyrical Ballads said the poems took "incidents and situations from common life" in "a selection of language really used by men."
In the Preface Wordsworth wrote that poetry is "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings" and "takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity."

title: The Romantics borrow the folk ballad
description: A ballad is a short narrative folk song re-created from memory at each performance; Coleridge's Rime of the Ancyent Marinere opened Lyrical Ballads in imitation of the old poets.
