facts.text: A ballad is a short narrative folk song, freshly re-created from memory at each performance and always open to variation.

Coleridge's The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere, the opening poem of Lyrical Ballads, was, as the 1798 Advertisement put it, "professedly written in imitation of the style, as well as of the spirit of the elder poets."

title: Wordsworth's daffodils
description: Dorothy Wordsworth's April 1802 journal entry on daffodils at Ullswater gave William the poem that opens "I wandered lonely as a Cloud".

facts.text: Dorothy Wordsworth's journal entry of April 1802 describing daffodils at Ullswater, in the Lake District, was used by William for his poem I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud.
Wordsworth's poem, published in 1807, opens: "I wandered lonely as a Cloud / That floats on high o'er Vales and Hills".

title: The Castle of Otranto
description: Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1764) is generally regarded as the first Gothic novel; it posed as a translated old Italian manuscript.

facts.text: Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto opens with a giant helmet falling from the sky and crushing Conrad, the lord's son, on his wedding day.
The Castle of Otranto, published in 1764, is generally regarded as the first Gothic novel and began the vogue for them.
Walpole first published the novel anonymously as the translation of an old Italian manuscript supposedly printed in Naples in 1529, and admitted he wrote it only in the second edition.

title: The Gothic toolkit
description: Gothic novels, named for medieval buildings and ruins, use castles, hidden passages and trapdoors to build mystery and terror, from Radcliffe's explained supernatural to Stoker's Dracula.

facts.text: Such fiction is called Gothic because its imaginative impulse was drawn from medieval buildings and ruins.
Gothic novels commonly use castles or monasteries with underground passages, dark battlements, hidden panels and trapdoors, and a prevailing atmosphere of mystery and terror.
Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho (1794) made her England's most popular novelist; her seemingly supernatural events are revealed as natural after a long delay.
Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897), written mainly as its characters' diaries and journals, follows a Transylvanian vampire who makes his way to England.

title: How Frankenstein began
description: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein grew from Byron's ghost story contest near Lake Geneva in 1816 and was published anonymously in January 1818, when she was 20.

facts.text: In the cold, stormy summer of 1816, near Lake Geneva in Switzerland, Lord Byron challenged his guests to a ghost story contest, which became the start of Frankenstein.
Mary Shelley published Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus anonymously in January 1818, when she was 20.
Frankenstein is about a scientist, Victor Frankenstein, who artificially creates a human being, and his creation brings tragedy into his life.

title: The Modern Prometheus
description: Frankenstein's subtitle recalls Prometheus, who in Greek myth stole fire for humans and was punished, and who in Ovid's Metamorphoses shapes the first humans from earth and water.

facts.text: In Greek myth Prometheus stole fire for humans, and Zeus punished him by having him fastened to a mountain in the Caucasus.
In Ovid's Metamorphoses, one account of the first people has Prometheus mix new earth with the water of new streams and shape man in the image of the gods.

title: Frankenstein and science fiction
description: Shelley dropped the Gothic's occult props for a scientist interested in galvanic electricity, which is why Frankenstein is often considered an early example of science fiction.

facts.text: Shelley dropped the occult trappings of the Gothic novel and made her hero a practicing scientist interested in galvanic electricity, one of the advanced technologies of the early 1800s.
Part Gothic novel and part philosophical novel, Frankenstein is often considered an early example of science fiction, and its champions call Shelley the mother of science fiction.

title: Dickens and the monthly part
description: Dickens's Pickwick Papers came out in monthly parts (1836 to 1837) and made him the most popular author of the day; serial publication shaped his plots, characters and bond with readers.

facts.text: The Pickwick Papers came out in monthly parts in 1836 and 1837, and within a few months it was the rage and Dickens the most popular author of the day.
Dickens found serialization congenial and profitable, repeated Pickwick's pattern of 20 monthly parts in later novels, and wrote Pickwick only weeks or days ahead of publication.
Serial publication encouraged multiple plots, required each episode to be shaped on its own, and produced an unprecedentedly close relationship between author and reader.
Dickens's powers of character creation and his ear for characteristic speech filled his novels with scores of characters.

title: Oliver Twist and poverty
description: Oliver Twist, serialized from 1837 to 1839, attacks the workhouse and shows how poverty nurtures crime; its starving hero asks for more gruel.

facts.text: In Oliver Twist, the starving workhouse boys cast lots over who will ask for more gruel; Oliver walks up to the master with his basin and says, "Please, sir, I want some more."
Oliver Twist, serialized in Bentley's Miscellany from 1837 to 1839, is centrally concerned with social evil (the workhouse and the criminal world) and illustrates how poverty nurtures crime.

title: Dickens reads aloud
description: From April 1858 Dickens gave paid public readings of his own work, having read for charity since 1853.

facts.text: Dickens gave occasional charity readings from 1853, and his paid public readings of his own work began in April 1858; he could earn more by reading than by writing.

title: The Brontës as the Bells
description: Charlotte, Emily and Anne Brontë published as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell to keep their secret and avoid reviewers' treatment of women; Jane Eyre (1847) was an immediate success.

facts.text: In 1846 Charlotte, Emily and Anne Brontë published Poems under the names Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell, and Charlotte kept Currer Bell for her novels.
The sisters took the pseudonyms to preserve secrecy and to avoid the special treatment they believed reviewers gave women.
Jane Eyre was published on October 16, 1847, and had an immediate success, far greater than the books her sisters published the same year.

title: Passionate inner voices
description: Jane Eyre speaks in her own first-person voice, a thinking, feeling woman; Emily's Wuthering Heights is a novel of passion and hate on the Yorkshire moors.

facts.text: Jane Eyre is told in the first person by Jane, an orphan who becomes a governess and falls in love with her employer, Mr. Rochester.
Charlotte Brontë's Jane is a thinking, feeling woman, craving love but able to renounce it at the call of principle.
Jane tells Rochester: "I am no bird; and no net ensnares me; I am a free human being with an independent will."
Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights (1847), published as Ellis Bell, is a highly imaginative work of passion and hate set on the Yorkshire moors.
Early critics found Wuthering Heights too savage, too animal-like and clumsy in construction.

title: Flaubert's Madame Bovary
description: Flaubert's Madame Bovary (1856), the story of a woman who shapes her life on romance novels, was told with unrelenting objectivity and put its author on trial.

facts.text: After Madame Bovary, subtitled Provincial Customs, ran in installments in 1856, the French government tried Flaubert for its alleged immorality, and he narrowly escaped conviction in 1857.
Emma Bovary destroys herself trying to base her life on ideas of passion and happiness taken from popular romance novels.
Flaubert spent about five years on Madame Bovary, searching for "le seul mot juste" (the one right word) and aiming at unrelenting objectivity, the dispassionate recording of every trait or incident.

title: What realism is
description: Realism is the accurate, unembellished depiction of contemporary life, portraying the ordinary lives of the middle and lower classes; it was a major trend in French novels from 1850 to 1880.

facts.text: Realism is the accurate, detailed, unembellished depiction of contemporary life; realists portrayed the lives of the middle and lower classes, the unexceptional and the ordinary.
Realism was a major trend in French novels and paintings between 1850 and 1880.

title: George Eliot's realism
description: Mary Ann Evans wrote as George Eliot; in Adam Bede she praised Dutch paintings of homely life over angels and heroes, and Middlemarch is A Study of Provincial Life.

facts.text: George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans; her novels include Adam Bede (1859) and Middlemarch, subtitled A Study of Provincial Life.

In chapter 17 of Adam Bede, Eliot praises Dutch paintings' "faithful pictures of a monotonous homely existence" and turns "from cloud-borne angels, from prophets, sibyls, and heroic warriors, to an old woman bending over her flower-pot."

title: War and Peace
description: War and Peace (1865 to 1869) weaves fictional families into the French invasion of Russia in 1812 and argues that great men do not shape history.

facts.text: Anna Karenina opens, in Constance Garnett's translation: "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way."
Tolstoy's War and Peace (1865 to 1869) begins in St. Petersburg in 1805 and centers on the French invasion of Russia in 1812.

War and Peace combines a historical account of the Napoleonic Wars, the lives of fictional characters such as Pierre Bezukhov, Prince Andrey Bolkonsky and the Rostovs, and essays on the philosophy of history.
In War and Peace, Tolstoy rejects the idea that history is shaped by great men and stresses the part ordinary people play.

title: Anna Karenina
description: Anna Karenina (1875 to 1877) sets Anna's affair with Vronsky, punished by a hypocritical high society, against Kitty and Levin's love story.

facts.text: Anna Karenina, published in installments between 1875 and 1877, centers on Anna's affair with Count Vronsky, with the courtship and marriage of Kitty and Levin as a counterpoint to her tragedy.
Anna pays not so much for breaking the moral code as for refusing to observe the proprieties that her hypocritical high society expects.

title: Raskolnikov's theory
description: In Crime and Punishment (1866) an impoverished former student kills an old pawnbroker, believing extraordinary people have the right to transgress.

facts.text: Dostoyevsky's Crime and Punishment was first published serially in 1866 and as a book in 1867.
Raskolnikov, an impoverished former student in St. Petersburg, decides to solve his problems at a stroke by murdering an old pawnbroker.
Raskolnikov theorizes that extraordinary people must have "the right to transgress," or progress would be impossible.

title: Guilt as the drama
description: Crime and Punishment follows Raskolnikov's psychological torment after the crime, Porfiry's psychological games, and his confession and slow repentance in Siberia.

facts.text: The novel follows Raskolnikov's descent into psychological torment as he struggles with his conscience and mounting suspicion.
The detective Porfiry Petrovich guesses Raskolnikov's guilt but cannot prove it, and plays psychological games with him.
Sonya persuades Raskolnikov to confess and follows him to Siberia, where he at first holds on to his theories before reaching repentance.

title: Ibsen's A Doll's House
description: Ibsen set moral drama in a realistic middle-class home; A Doll's House (1879) ends with Nora leaving her family and slamming the door.

facts.text: A Doll's House (1879) ends as Nora declares her independence and leaves her husband and children, slamming the door of the house behind her.
Nora had secretly forged a signature to get the money that saved her husband Torvald's life; when it comes out, he turns on her out of concern for his reputation.
Ibsen placed his moral analysis against a severely realistic middle-class background.

title: Chekhov's quiet stage
description: Chekhov's plays show the day-to-day life of Russian landowners with the big events offstage; The Seagull flopped in 1896 and triumphed in 1898; The Cherry Orchard (1904) ends with axes offstage.

facts.text: Chekhov's plays about the day-to-day life of Russia's landed gentry achieved a delicate poetic realism.
Most of the climactic action in Chekhov's plays takes place offstage.
The Seagull was badly received at its 1896 premiere but succeeded when the new Moscow Art Theatre staged it in 1898.

In The Cherry Orchard (1904) a family's estate is sold to pay its debts and bought by the merchant Lopakhin; the play ends with axes heard offstage cutting down the orchard, and Chekhov called it a comedy.

title: A century of installments
description: Many major 19th-century novels, from Oliver Twist to Madame Bovary, Crime and Punishment and Anna Karenina, first reached readers in installments.

facts.text: Madame Bovary ran in installments in the Revue de Paris in 1856, Crime and Punishment was serialized in 1866, and Anna Karenina came out in installments between 1875 and 1877.

title: Poe's single effect
description: In his 1842 review of Hawthorne, Poe argued that a tale should be built backward from one preconceived effect, with every word serving it.

facts.text: In May 1842, reviewing Nathaniel Hawthorne's Twice-Told Tales in Graham's Magazine, Edgar Allan Poe set out his theory of the prose tale.
Poe wrote that a skilful writer first conceives "a certain unique or single effect", then invents the incidents that best bring it about, with no word that does not serve that one design.
Poe wrote: "If his very initial sentence tend not to the outbringing of this effect, then he has failed in his first step."
In "The Philosophy of Composition" (1846), Poe claimed "The Raven" proceeded step by step "with the precision and rigid consequence of a mathematical problem".
Poe said he settled on a melancholy tone first and then chose the refrain "Nevermore" to fit it.
Many anthologies credit Poe as the "architect" of the modern short story.

title: One sitting: why Poe preferred the short tale
description: Poe held that a tale read in one sitting, a half-hour to two hours, keeps its full effect, while a novel loses it to interruptions.

facts.text: Poe described the prose tale as a short narrative "requiring from a half-hour to one or two hours in its perusal".
Poe argued that the novel, because it "cannot be read at one sitting", loses "the immense force derivable from totality", since worldly interests intrude in the pauses.

title: The Scarlet Letter's Puritan story
description: Hawthorne's 1850 novel frames a tale of Puritan Boston: Hester Prynne, made to wear a scarlet A, refuses to name her child's father.

facts.text: Hawthorne worked at the Salem Custom House, and in the introduction to The Scarlet Letter he describes it and pretends to find the story among a previous surveyor's papers.
In the introduction, the narrator finds a rag of scarlet cloth shaped like the capital letter A.

The Scarlet Letter (1850) is set among the Puritans of 17th-century Boston, where Hester Prynne, who has had a child outside marriage, must wear a scarlet A for adultery and refuses to name the father.

title: A symbol that changes meaning
description: Hester's embroidered A, meant to shame her, comes to mean Able to many; Hawthorne, descended from a Salem witch-trial judge, turns it on the Puritan past.

facts.text: Hester's A is of fine red cloth, "surrounded with an elaborate embroidery and fantastic flourishes of gold-thread".
Because of her helpfulness, many people refused to read the A in its original sense: "They said that it meant Able; so strong was Hester Prynne, with a woman's strength."
Hawthorne's ancestor John Hathorne was a magistrate and the stern interrogator of the accused witches at Salem, and Hawthorne was haunted by such ancestors, who appear in his fiction.
In the introduction Hawthorne writes that, as his persecuting ancestors' representative, he takes "shame upon myself for their sakes".

title: Ahab's obsession
description: Captain Ahab turns the Pequod's whaling voyage into a revenge hunt for the white whale that took his leg, and the hunt destroys the ship.

facts.text: Captain Ahab of the Pequod lost his leg to the white whale Moby Dick: "it was Moby Dick that dismasted me".
Ishmael says Ahab "seemed ready to sacrifice all mortal interests to that one passion", the capture of Moby Dick.
In the final chase Ahab cries "from hell's heart I stab at thee", the whale destroys the Pequod, and only Ishmael survives.

title: How Moby-Dick was made
description: Melville drew on his whaling voyage and the wreck of the Essex, and, spurred by Hawthorne, turned a sea story into an epic novel that flopped, then was rediscovered.

facts.text: Moby-Dick (1851) opens with the sentence "Call me Ishmael."
In January 1841, at 21, Herman Melville sailed from New Bedford on the whaleship Acushnet, a voyage he drew on for Moby-Dick.
Melville has Ishmael call a whale ship "my Yale College and my Harvard".
Moby-Dick is described as Melville's "epic novel", whose many layers were not fully appreciated until the 1920s.
Hawthorne is widely credited with inspiring Melville to turn early drafts of a sea adventure into Moby-Dick, which Melville dedicated to him.
In 1820 a sperm whale rammed and sank the Nantucket whaleship Essex; Melville first heard the story aboard the Acushnet, and it shaped Moby-Dick.
Moby-Dick was a critical and commercial failure and was not rediscovered until the 1920s.

title: Douglass and the pathway to freedom
description: When his enslaver banned his reading lessons, Douglass understood that reading was a pathway from slavery to freedom, and he kept learning in secret.

facts.text: In Baltimore, Sophia Auld began teaching the young Frederick Douglass "the A, B, C" and then helped him spell short words.
Mr. Auld forbade the lessons, saying reading "would forever unfit him to be a slave".
Douglass wrote: "From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom," an instruction he said he had gained by accident from his master.
Douglass made the white boys he met in the street his teachers, giving bread for "that more valuable bread of knowledge".
Douglass learned to write letters from those ship carpenters wrote on timber, such as L for larboard and S for starboard.
At twelve, Douglass got The Columbian Orator, a collection of speeches and writings on natural rights.

title: The 1845 Narrative, written by himself
description: After escaping in 1838, Douglass published his Narrative in 1845, full of names and places and titled Written by Himself, to answer doubters.

facts.text: Douglass escaped slavery in 1838, disguised as a sailor.
Some audiences suspected Douglass had never been enslaved, so in 1845 he published his Narrative, with names and places, to lay those doubts to rest.
The 1845 title page reads "Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave. Written by Himself."

title: Leaves of Grass, the book Whitman kept rewriting
description: Whitman self-published twelve untitled poems in 1855 and kept expanding Leaves of Grass through edition after edition until his death in 1892.

facts.text: Walt Whitman worked as a printer and newspaper journalist in Brooklyn through the 1850s.
Whitman published the first Leaves of Grass himself in 1855: twelve untitled poems and a preface, one of them later famous as "Song of Myself".
Whitman kept refining Leaves of Grass through several editions; the second (1856) had thirty-two poems, and he worked on the "deathbed edition" of 1891-92 until his death in 1892.

title: Whitman's all-including 'I'
description: Whitman's 'myself' grows to include every reader, and his long unrhymed catalogs list Americans at work to hold the whole country.

facts.text: Song of Myself opens: "I celebrate myself, and sing myself, / And what I assume you shall assume, / For every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you."
In Song of Myself Whitman writes: "Do I contradict myself? / Very well then I contradict myself, / (I am large, I contain multitudes.)"
In "I Hear America Singing", Whitman lists mechanics, the carpenter, the mason, the boatman, the shoemaker and more, "Each singing what belongs to him or her and to none else".
The National Park Service calls Whitman's style experimental, "a free-verse avalanche in celebration of nature and self", and a distinctly American voice.

title: Dickinson's small poems, large ideas
description: Dickinson packed death, hope and eternity into short poems in hymn-like common meter, often with slant rhyme.

facts.text: Dickinson's verse is often associated with common meter, alternating lines of eight and six syllables, often used in hymns such as "Amazing Grace".
The 1890s editions print: "Because I could not stop for Death, / He kindly stopped for me; / The carriage held but just ourselves / And Immortality."
Rhyme that is not perfect is called slant rhyme; Dickinson used it often, when it was less common among her contemporaries.
The 1890s editions print: "Hope is the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul, / And sings the tune without the words, / And never stops at all,"

title: Dickinson's hidden poems and her dashes
description: Almost none of her nearly 1,800 poems were published in her life; her family found them in handmade booklets, and early editors removed her dashes.

facts.text: Emily Dickinson composed almost 1,800 poems, but fewer than a dozen were published in her lifetime.
After Dickinson died in 1886, her family discovered forty handbound booklets of poems, which she made by folding and sewing stationery and copying poems into them.
Dickinson most often punctuated with dashes, and her handwritten poems show dash-like marks of various sizes and directions, some even vertical.

Her poems were first published, from 1890, according to the taste of early editors, who removed her marks; the standard version today prints her dashes as en dashes, a closer approximation to her intention.

title: Huck's own voice
description: Twain let a barely schooled boy narrate a whole novel in his own speech, a break with polished narrators that writers such as Hemingway saw as the start of modern American writing.

facts.text: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn opens with a notice: "persons attempting to find a moral in it will be banished; persons attempting to find a plot in it will be shot."
Huck narrates from the first line: "You don't know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain't no matter."

Critic Tony Tanner wrote that the book was revolutionary because a child narrates all of it in the vernacular, where earlier vernacular characters had always been framed by a more sophisticated adult voice.
Ernest Hemingway declared that all modern American literature comes from one book by Mark Twain, Huckleberry Finn.
Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn was published in 1885 in the United States.

title: Huck, Jim and the debate over the book
description: Huck's decision to help Jim is read by defenders as satire of a racist society; critics object to the book's slur and its portrayal of Jim, and schools still argue.

facts.text: The novel follows the friendship of Huck, a poor white boy, and Jim, a man who has escaped slavery.
Believing that helping Jim is a sin, Huck tears up a letter that would betray him, saying "All right, then, I'll go to hell."
Defenders of the novel read it as a satire in which Twain exposed the hypocrisy of the society he grew up in.
Soon after publication, the book was banned in Concord, Massachusetts.
Critics object to the book's repeated use of a racial slur and to its portrayal of Jim along the lines of the minstrel show.
In 2000, scholar Jocelyn Chadwick defended teaching the novel, while the Pennsylvania NAACP and professor Jonathan Arac wanted it off required reading lists.
Satire or Evasion? (1992) collects essays by African American scholars, from laudatory to openly hostile, on whether the book succeeds as satire of racism.

title: Hughes's blues poems
description: Langston Hughes, a leading voice of the Harlem Renaissance, built poems on the rhythms of blues and jazz and the everyday speech of Black America.

facts.text: Langston Hughes's "The Weary Blues" begins: "Droning a drowsy syncopated tune, / Rocking back and forth to a mellow croon,"
Hughes's first book of poems, The Weary Blues, was published in 1926.
The Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s celebrated African American culture and achievement, and Hughes became a fixture of it.
Hughes said the people he met were the influences of his work, but blues and jazz were its rhythm.
Hughes wanted to tell his people's stories in ways that reflected their actual culture, including their love of music, laughter and language.
Hughes cited Paul Laurence Dunbar, Carl Sandburg and Walt Whitman as his primary influences.

title: Hurston's folklore and speech
description: Zora Neale Hurston, raised in all-Black Eatonville, collected Black Southern folklore as an anthropologist and wrote Their Eyes Were Watching God in its speech.

facts.text: Zora Neale Hurston grew up in Eatonville, Florida, established in 1887 as the nation's first incorporated Black township, where people told colorful stories on the village store porch.
Hurston studied anthropology with Franz Boas at Barnard College and went back to Florida to collect folklore.
Hurston's Mules and Men (1935) is a collection of Black Southern folklore.
In Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), every character speaks Southern African American Vernacular English, set against standard English narration.

title: The history behind Beloved
description: Morrison built Beloved from the 1856 case of Margaret Garner, then changed its ending and told it from the inside, as fiction rather than a retelling.

facts.text: In 1856 Margaret Garner, an enslaved woman who had escaped to Cincinnati, was about to be returned to Kentucky under fugitive slave laws and killed her infant daughter rather than see her returned to slavery.
Garner was charged not with murder but with destruction of her owner's property.
Morrison came across the Garner case in an 1856 newspaper clipping while compiling The Black Book (1974).
Beloved changes history: Sethe and Denver end the novel alive and free, while Margaret Garner was recaptured and died in captivity.
Morrison said that focusing on the characters' interior lives puts authority back in the hands of the enslaved rather than the slaveholder.

title: Beloved and memory
description: Beloved's haunted house and broken time scheme show a past that will not stay buried.

facts.text: Toni Morrison's Beloved (1987) opens at 124 Bluestone Road, a house where chairs move by themselves, kettles turn over and handprints appear in cake icing.
The novel opens in 1873 in Cincinnati, where Sethe, who escaped slavery, believes the ghost is her older daughter, who died before she was two.
A mysterious young woman named Beloved appears, the age Sethe's dead daughter would have been, and Sethe takes her in.
Beloved moves between its Reconstruction-era present and flashbacks from before Emancipation, a non-linear structure of fractured memory in which the characters work daily at beating back the past.

title: More American voices
description: American literature reaches beyond this chapter: Native storytellers and writers such as Zitkála-Šá and N. Scott Momaday, and James Baldwin of Harlem.

facts.text: In "The School Days of an Indian Girl", in American Indian Stories (1921), Zitkála-Šá recalls a school cutting off her braids: "Then I lost my spirit."
Zitkála-Šá was a writer and a member of the Yankton Dakota Sioux.
N. Scott Momaday, a Kiowa writer, won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for his first novel, House Made of Dawn (1969).
James Baldwin, born in Harlem in 1924, published his first novel, Go Tell It on the Mountain, in 1953.
Baldwin preached as a teenager, and many note the cadences of the church and the Bible in his style.

title: Modernism: make it new
description: Modernism, a period of experiment in the arts, took hold in literature after World War I, whose enormity shook faith in Western culture; writers answered with fragments and new forms under Pound's slogan "make it new".

facts.text: Ezra Pound used Make It New as the title of his 1934 collection of essays, and the phrase became the all-purpose label for modernist novelty.
Pound's phrase comes from an anecdote about Tang, first king of the Shang dynasty, who was said to have had a washbasin inscribed with the slogan.
Modernism was a period of experiment in the arts from the late 19th to the mid-20th century; as a literary movement it is tied above all to the years after World War I (1914 to 1918).
The enormity of World War I undermined faith in the foundations of Western society and culture, and postwar modernist literature reflects disillusionment and fragmentation.

Modernist writers challenged the conventions of the whole post-Romantic era with radical experiments, such as stream of consciousness and fragmentary images and allusions, asking readers to take an active role in interpreting.

title: Joyce's Ulysses and the Odyssey
description: Ulysses (Paris, 1922) follows three Dubliners through June 16, 1904, and parallels Homer's Odyssey, suggesting ordinary modern lives matter as much as heroes'.

facts.text: James Joyce's Ulysses and T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land were both published in 1922, landmarks of modernist literature.
Ulysses was first published in Paris on February 2, 1922, and follows three Dubliners through a single day, June 16, 1904.
Ulysses parallels Homer's Odyssey (Leopold Bloom is Odysseus, Stephen Dedalus is Telemachus, Molly Bloom is Penelope), making the point that ordinary modern lives matter as much as heroes'.

title: War poets and "the old Lie"
description: Horace's line that dying for your country is sweet and fitting met two answers in World War I: Rupert Brooke's idealistic sonnets and Wilfred Owen's Dulce et Decorum Est, which calls it the old Lie.

facts.text: The Latin line "Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori" comes from the Roman poet Horace's Odes and means it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country.
Rupert Brooke's war sonnets, published as 1914 and Other Poems in 1915, brought him immediate fame and express an idealism in the face of death.
Brooke's "The Soldier" begins: "If I should die, think only this of me: / That there's some corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England."
Brooke died of blood poisoning (septicemia) on a hospital ship off the Greek island of Skyros on April 23, 1915, on his way to the Dardanelles.
Britannica describes the idealism of Brooke's war sonnets as in strong contrast to the later poetry of trench warfare.
Wilfred Owen drafted Dulce et Decorum Est in 1917 at Craiglockhart War Hospital, where he was being treated for shell shock.
Dulce et Decorum Est describes a gas attack like the one Owen himself experienced early in 1917.
Owen's poem opens "Bent double, like old beggars under sacks," and ends by calling Horace's line "The old Lie: Dulce et decorum est / Pro patria mori."

title: Owen's poetry of pity
description: Owen, killed a week before the Armistice with few poems in print, wrote in the 1920 preface to his Poems that the book was not about heroes: "The Poetry is in the pity."

facts.text: Owen was killed on November 4, 1918, leading his men across the Sambre-Oise canal at Ors; the news reached his parents on November 11, Armistice Day.
Few of Owen's poems appeared in print during his lifetime; his collected poems were first published in 1920, after his death.
The preface to Owen's Poems (1920) begins "This book is not about heroes." and says "The Poetry is in the pity."

title: The Waste Land: fragments and borrowed voices
description: Eliot's The Waste Land (1922) is a 433-line, five-part poem built from fragments, allusions and other languages, with Tiresias, drawn from Ovid, uniting its voices.

facts.text: The Waste Land opens: "April is the cruellest month, breeding / Lilacs out of the dead land".
The Waste Land was first published in 1922, in The Criterion in London (October) and then in The Dial in New York (November).
The Waste Land is a 433-line poem in five parts.
The poem weaves in allusions to Chaucer, Dante, Shakespeare, classical literature and myth, the Bible and the Upanishads.
Near its end, The Waste Land says: "These fragments I have shored against my ruins".
The poem ends with the Sanskrit "Shantih shantih shantih", which Eliot's note calls a formal ending to an Upanishad.
Tiresias, a figure from Greek myth who is blind but can see the future, is a key presence in The Waste Land.

Eliot's notes call Tiresias the most important personage in the poem, uniting all the rest, say "What Tiresias sees, in fact, is the substance of the poem," quote Ovid's Latin on Tiresias, and cite Ovid's Metamorphoses for Philomela.

title: Why The Waste Land felt hard
description: Pound cut the manuscript to nearly half; the book edition added Eliot's notes; critics denounced its obscurity and praised its Modernism, and Eliot's first note points readers to Weston's Grail book.

facts.text: After its magazine appearances, The Waste Land came out as a book with footnotes by Eliot.
Ezra Pound helped condense the poem's original manuscript to nearly half its size.
The poem's complex, erudite style was denounced for its obscurity and praised for its Modernism.
Eliot's first note says Jessie L. Weston's book on the Grail legend, From Ritual to Romance, "will elucidate the difficulties of the poem much better than my notes can do".

title: Stream of consciousness
description: A technique for rendering the flow of impressions, memories and associations in a character's mind, often ignoring orderly sentences; the phrase comes from William James (1890). Molly Bloom's monologue ends Ulysses.

facts.text: Ulysses (1922) ends with Molly Bloom's monologue, a direct first-person expression of her thoughts, apparently free of the author's selection and control.
The last words of Ulysses are "yes I said yes I will Yes."
The psychologist William James used the phrase stream of consciousness in The Principles of Psychology (1890).
In fiction, stream of consciousness is a technique that tries to render the flow of impressions (sights, sounds, feelings, associations) passing through one person's mind.
Stream of consciousness commonly ignores orderly sentence structure and lets in fragments of thought.
Interior monologue is often used as another name for stream of consciousness, but it may be limited to a character's organized, rational thoughts, while the stream lets in every half thought.

title: Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway
description: Mrs. Dalloway (1925) follows Clarissa Dalloway through one London day, moving between minds (Clarissa's, the shell-shocked Septimus's) as memories break in and Big Ben marks the hours.

facts.text: Virginia Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway (1925) follows Clarissa Dalloway through one day in London as she prepares a party, with Big Ben marking the time.
Mrs. Dalloway opens: "Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself."
On the first page, a squeak of hinges she can hear now carries Clarissa back to Bourton, when she was a girl of eighteen.

Woolf's stream-of-consciousness narration moves fluidly between characters' thoughts, including those of Septimus Warren Smith, a World War I veteran with shell shock; she was influenced by Joyce's Ulysses.
When Big Ben strikes in Mrs. Dalloway, the phrase "The leaden circles dissolved in the air" recurs.

title: Kafka's transformation
description: Kafka's Die Verwandlung (1915): Gregor Samsa wakes as a monstrous vermin whose kind is left vague. Kafka knew Ovid's Metamorphoses but chose the German word for transformation.

facts.text: Kafka's story was first published in German as Die Verwandlung in 1915: Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, wakes one morning changed in his bed into a gigantic insect.
Gregor's first worry on waking is work: missing it and disappointing his demanding boss.
Kafka had translated part of Ovid's Metamorphoses at school, yet he titled his story Die Verwandlung ("the transformation"), not Die Metamorphose.
Kafka's first sentence calls Gregor an "ungeheueren Ungeziefer", roughly "monstrous vermin", and he kept the creature's exact kind ambiguous.
Kafka told his publisher that the insect itself must not be drawn on the cover, not even from a distance.

title: Two readings of The Metamorphosis
description: Readers weigh Kafka's story through the family (the Samsas' rejection; Kafka's letter to his domineering father) and through work (Gregor, the sole provider, thinks first of his train and his job).

facts.text: Gregor is his family's sole provider; their response moves from shock to rejection, and his sister, who first cares for him, finally insists they must get rid of the monster.
In 1919 Kafka wrote a long letter to his domineering father that was never sent; Britannica says it reveals the background of the father-son conflict in many of his stories.
On waking, Gregor frets that he has missed the five o'clock train and that the next one leaves at seven.
Scholars read Gregor's transformation through several lenses, among them family alienation and the dehumanizing effects of labor.

title: Gatsby and the American Dream
description: The Great Gatsby (1925): self-made Jay Gatsby reaches for Daisy and the past. Britannica reads it as a pessimistic look at the American Dream; Nick also praises Gatsby's gift for hope.

facts.text: F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, is narrated by Nick Carraway.
Gatsby tells Daisy, "You always have a green light that burns all night at the end of your dock."

Jay Gatsby is a self-made millionaire from humble roots, born James Gatz, who grew rich bootlegging during Prohibition and pursues Daisy Buchanan, whom he loved in his youth, though she married Tom Buchanan.
When Nick says "You can't repeat the past," Gatsby answers: "Can't repeat the past? Why of course you can!"
Britannica reads the novel as a pessimistic examination of the American Dream, showing how materialism corrupts ambition, with the green light standing for Gatsby's unattainable dream.
The Great Gatsby ends: "So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past."

Nick praises Gatsby's "extraordinary gift for hope, a romantic readiness such as I have never found in any other person" and says Gatsby "turned out all right at the end"; it was the "foul dust" that floated in the wake of his dreams that preyed on him.

title: The Lost Generation
description: Gertrude Stein's name for American writers, Fitzgerald among them, who came of age in World War I and made their names in the 1920s, disillusioned; Gatsby sold poorly in 1925 and is now a classic.

facts.text: The Lost Generation were American writers who came of age during World War I and made their names in the 1920s, disillusioned with postwar society; F. Scott Fitzgerald was one.
Gertrude Stein is credited with the phrase; Hemingway used her remark "You are all a lost generation" as the epigraph of The Sun Also Rises (1926).
The Great Gatsby was not a commercial success when it was published in 1925; it is now considered a classic of American literature.

title: Tagore's Gitanjali
description: Gitanjali (Song Offerings, 1912): Tagore's own English prose versions of Bengali religious songs, introduced by Yeats. Tagore wrote more than 2,000 songs, including the anthems of India and Bangladesh.

facts.text: The English Gitanjali (1912) is Tagore's own prose translations of religious poems from several of his Bengali verse collections.
The English Gitanjali is subtitled Song Offerings and describes itself as prose translations made by the author from the original Bengali, with an introduction by W. B. Yeats.
Poem 35 of the English Gitanjali begins: "Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high;".
Tagore composed more than 2,000 songs, popular among all classes of Bengali society, and wrote the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh.
Yeats's introduction reports a Bengali doctor saying Tagore's songs "are sung from the west of India into Burma wherever Bengali is spoken," and says Tagore "writes music for his words".

title: Tagore's 1913 Nobel Prize
description: In 1913 Tagore became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, cited for verse made part of Western literature "in his own English words"; Yeats noted what translation lost.

facts.text: In 1913 Rabindranath Tagore became the first non-European to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.
The 1913 prize motivation praises Tagore's verse, "by which, with consummate skill, he has made his poetic thought, expressed in his own English words, a part of the literature of the West".
Yeats writes that the lyrics in the original Bengali, his Indian friends told him, are full of subtlety of rhythm and "untranslatable delicacies of colour".

title: Things Fall Apart
description: Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958), written in English and peppered with Igbo proverbs, follows Okonkwo as missionaries and colonial rule arrive in the 1890s; its title comes from Yeats.

facts.text: Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart, written in English and published in 1958, follows Okonkwo, a leader of an Igbo community, as white missionaries and colonial government intrude in the 1890s.
Traditionally structured and peppered with Igbo proverbs, the novel describes the simultaneous disintegration of Okonkwo and of his village.
The novel's title comes from W. B. Yeats's poem "The Second Coming": "Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold;".
Things Fall Apart helped create the Nigerian literary renaissance of the 1960s.

title: Achebe writing back
description: Achebe resented colonial stereotypes of Africa (Cary's Mister Johnson, the "heart of darkness") and wanted his novels to show readers their past had not been an age of savagery; his District Commissioner shrinks Okonkwo to a paragraph.

facts.text: At the end of Things Fall Apart, the District Commissioner thinks Okonkwo's story might fill a paragraph in the book he plans to call The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger.

Achebe resented the stereotype of Africa as an undifferentiated primitive land, the "heart of darkness," and novels like Joyce Cary's Mister Johnson, with its comic African who adores his white colonial boss.

In his essay "The Novelist as Teacher", Achebe said he would be satisfied if his novels set in the past taught readers that their past, imperfect as it was, had not been an age of savagery from which Europeans rescued them.

title: Magical realism
description: The matter-of-fact inclusion of fantastic or mythical elements in otherwise realistic fiction, above all in Latin America; the term began with Franz Roh's writing on painting in 1925.

facts.text: Magic realism is the matter-of-fact inclusion of fantastic or mythical elements in seemingly realistic fiction, associated above all with Latin American writers such as García Márquez, Jorge Luis Borges, Julio Cortázar and Isabel Allende.
The term magic realism was coined in 1925 by the German critic Franz Roh to describe modern realist paintings with fantasy or dreamlike subjects.
In magical realism the characters who meet magic treat it as normal; in One Hundred Years of Solitude, magic rarely warrants surprise.

title: García Márquez and Macondo
description: One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967) follows seven generations of Buendías in Macondo, a town based on Aracataca, telling miracles in the deadpan way García Márquez's grandmother told stories.

facts.text: In One Hundred Years of Solitude, Remedios the Beauty ascends to heaven one day while hanging sheets to dry.

Gabriel García Márquez published One Hundred Years of Solitude (Cien años de soledad) in Spanish in 1967; it follows seven generations of the Buendía family in the fictional Colombian town of Macondo.
Macondo is based on Aracataca, García Márquez's hometown in Colombia.
In the novel it rains for four years, eleven months and two days, and yellow butterflies always accompany the young man Mauricio Babilonia.
García Márquez said his grandmother told fantastic, supernatural stories without changing her expression, and that he wrote the novel by believing the stories himself and telling them the same way.

title: What modern writers changed, and why
description: Modern writers broke forms (fragments, the flow of thought) after World War I shook faith in Western culture, and writers from beyond Europe changed who tells the story.

facts.text: In this chapter's works, two causes of change stand out: World War I's blow to faith in Western culture, and writers such as Achebe setting out to correct others' stories of their people's past.

title: Three Cinderellas
description: Perrault's Cinderella (1697) has a glass slipper, a godmother and forgiveness; the Grimms' has a hazel tree, a golden slipper and blinded stepsisters.

facts.text: The glass slipper by which the prince recognizes Cinderella is unique to Perrault's version; other versions often use a golden or silver slipper or a ring.
Perrault's Cinderella (Cendrillon) appeared in 1697 in his collection Contes de ma mère l'oye, Tales of Mother Goose.
In Perrault's Cinderella, a fairy godmother gives her glass slippers, and at the end Cinderella forgives her stepsisters and matches them with two great lords of the court.

In the Grimms' Cinderella, a hazel tree on her mother's grave and a white bird grant her wishes, the slipper is golden, the stepsisters cut off a toe and a heel to fit it, and pigeons peck out their eyes.

title: Why fairy-tale versions differ
description: Perrault retold old tales to amuse his children; the Grimms took most of theirs from oral sources and tried to keep the tellers' words; Andersen invented almost all of his.

facts.text: Perrault's Mother Goose tales retold half-forgotten folk tales in a simple style and were written to amuse his children.
The Grimms' Children's and Household Tales (1812 to 1822) took most of its stories from oral sources, aiming at a genuine reproduction of the teller's words and ways.
All but a dozen of Hans Christian Andersen's 156 fairy tales are his own creations.
Andersen's first book of tales appeared in 1835; he used the idioms of the spoken language, breaking with literary tradition, and some of his tales are deeply pessimistic and end unhappily.

title: How Alice began
description: Lewis Carroll (Charles Dodgson, an Oxford mathematics lecturer) told the Alice story to the Liddell children on July 4, 1862; it was published in 1865 with Tenniel's pictures.

facts.text: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland opens with Alice peeping into her sister's book: "and what is the use of a book," thought Alice "without pictures or conversations?"
Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, a lecturer in mathematics at Christ Church, Oxford.
On July 4, 1862, Dodgson rowed the three Liddell children up the Thames and told them the tale of Alice; Alice Liddell asked him to write it down.
Alice's Adventures in Wonderland was published in 1865, illustrated by John Tenniel.

title: Alice laughs at moral lessons
description: Alice appeared when children's books were meant to teach morals; Carroll parodied moral verses and gave morals to the silly Duchess.

facts.text: Alice at first baffled critics: it appeared when children's literature was generally intended to teach moral lessons.

Carroll's "How doth the little crocodile / Improve his shining tail" parodies Isaac Watts's moral poem "Against Idleness and Mischief" (1715), which begins "How doth the little busy bee / Improve each shining hour".
Carroll's crocodile welcomes little fishes in "With gently smiling jaws".
The Duchess tells Alice, "Everything's got a moral, if only you can find it," and Alice thinks, "How fond she is of finding morals in things!"
By the end of the 19th century, Alice had become the most popular children's book in England.

title: Dupin and Holmes
description: Poe's "The Murders in the Rue Morgue" (1841) made the pattern: a brilliant reasoner and a narrating friend; Holmes and Watson (1887) followed it.

facts.text: In A Study in Scarlet, Watson tells Holmes he reminds him of Poe's Dupin, and Holmes replies, "Dupin was a very inferior fellow."

Edgar Allan Poe's "The Murders in the Rue Morgue", published in April 1841, is called the first detective story: the amateur C. Auguste Dupin solves a sealed-room murder by reasoning from the clues, and his nameless friend narrates.
Sherlock Holmes and his companion Dr. Watson, who narrates, first appeared in Arthur Conan Doyle's A Study in Scarlet (1887).

title: Fair play in detective fiction
description: Clues should reach the reader when they reach the detective; Knox's 1929 rules add that the criminal must appear early and every clue be shown at once.

facts.text: It is usually axiomatic in detective fiction that the clues leading to a logical solution be fairly presented to the reader at the same time the detective receives them.

In 1929 Ronald Knox set out ten rules for detective fiction, including that the criminal must be someone mentioned early in the story and that the detective must not find any clue not instantly shown to the reader.

Holmes greets Watson with "You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive," and later explains the clues: a medical man with a military air, a face dark from the tropics but fair wrists, a haggard face and a stiffly held, injured left arm.

title: Verne: space travel as engineering
description: Verne's From the Earth to the Moon (1865) fired travelers at the Moon from a giant cannon and was the first fiction to treat space travel as an engineering problem.

facts.text: Science fiction deals principally with the impact of actual or imagined science upon society or individuals.
In Jules Verne's From the Earth to the Moon (1865), members of the Baltimore Gun Club build an enormous cannon to shoot a "space-bullet" to the Moon from Florida.
From the Earth to the Moon was the first fiction to treat space travel as a coherent engineering problem, recognizing for example that there could be no air.
Verne found no plausible way to land his cannon-fired passengers; in the sequel, Round the Moon (1870), they whiz past the Moon, cataloging craters.

title: Wells: the future as a mirror of society
description: H. G. Wells used science-fiction what-ifs to look at society: The Time Machine's Eloi and Morlocks stand for the leisure and working classes.

facts.text: H. G. Wells studied biology under T. H. Huxley and became a science teacher.
In Wells's The Time Machine (1895), the Time Traveller reaches the year 802,701 and finds the gentle Eloi above ground and the Morlocks below, who prey on them.
In The Time Machine, the Eloi stand for the leisure class and the Morlocks for the working class.
In Wells's The War of the Worlds (1898), invading Martians are killed by Earth's bacteria, against which they have no defense.
Britannica sets Wells's imagination apart from the "comparatively mechanical anticipations of Jules Verne".

title: Dystopias as warnings
description: A dystopia inverts More's utopia (1516): a society of dehumanization, fear and oppression, written as a cautionary tale about present trends.

facts.text: Thomas More coined the word utopia in his 1516 book Utopia, a play on Greek meaning both "good place" and "no place".
A dystopian novel depicts a fictional society marked by dehumanization, fear and oppression; such novels often serve as cautionary tales, projecting current trends into a grim future.
Britannica calls Brave New World and Nineteen Eighty-Four great didactic landmarks that can help correct illiberal tendencies.

title: Control by pleasure or by fear
description: Huxley's Brave New World (1932) controls people with conditioning and the drug soma; Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) with surveillance and fear.

facts.text: In Aldous Huxley's Brave New World (1932), citizens are sorted as embryos into castes from Alphas to Epsilons, conditioned for their roles, and kept content and compliant with the drug soma.

George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), a warning against totalitarianism, shows a Party ruling through the Thought Police and continual surveillance, with Newspeak designed to limit free thought.

In Amusing Ourselves to Death (1985), Neil Postman wrote that Orwell feared those who would ban books, Huxley that no one would want to read them: Orwell's danger is what we hate, Huxley's what we love.

title: Tolkien's Norse borrowings
description: Tolkien, an Oxford scholar of Old English, took dwarf names like Durin and Thorin from the Poetic Edda and modeled Gandalf on the wandering Odin.

facts.text: Many dwarf names in Tolkien, including Durin, Bombur, Nori and Thorin, match names of dwarves in the Völuspá, a poem of the Poetic Edda.
J. R. R. Tolkien taught at Oxford from 1925 to 1959, specializing in Old and Middle English, and gave a landmark 1936 lecture on Beowulf.
Tolkien's The Hobbit appeared in 1937 and The Lord of the Rings in 1954 to 1955.
In his letters, Tolkien described an ambition to create a mythology for England.
Gandalf's likely model is Odin, who in Norse poems travels among humans as a wandering wizard, coming and going with his own purposes.

title: The stolen cup: Beowulf and The Hobbit
description: Bilbo's theft of a cup from Smaug echoes the stolen cup that wakes Beowulf's dragon; Tolkien called Beowulf a valued source but said the scene arose naturally.

facts.text: In Beowulf, a dragon is enraged when a man steals from its treasure hoard; in J. Lesslie Hall's translation it misses its "gem-cup" and ravages the land with fire.
In The Hobbit, Bilbo carries off a great two-handled cup from the hoard of the sleeping dragon Smaug, who wakes in fury.
In a 1938 letter to the Observer, Tolkien called Beowulf among his most valued sources, but said it was not consciously in his mind as he wrote the theft, which arose naturally from the story.

title: Prose or verse: Butler and Pope
description: Butler's Odyssey (1900) is prose and keeps Homer's repeated formulas visible; Pope's (1725 to 1726) is rhymed couplets and varies them.

facts.text: Odyssey Book II opens in Samuel Butler's translation "Now when the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared"; in Pope's, "Now reddening from the dawn, the morning ray / Glow'd in the front of heaven".
Samuel Butler's Odyssey, first published in 1900, renders Homer into English prose; his preface says that much that is right in poetry is wrong in prose.
Pope's Odyssey (1725 to 1726), a job shared with William Broome and Elijah Fenton, is written in rhyming heroic couplets of 10-syllable lines.
Pope's Odyssey renders Homer's recurring dawn in varying words rather than one fixed phrase; Book II, for example, opens "Now reddening from the dawn".

title: One word, several pictures
description: The Odyssey's first description of Odysseus, polytropos, can mean much-wandering or wily; each translator chooses which picture to stress.

facts.text: The Odyssey's first line calls Odysseus polytropos, which can mean much-travelled or much-wandering, or figuratively turning many ways: versatile, wily.

Butler opens the Odyssey "Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide"; Pope opens "The man for wisdom's various arts renown'd", with "Wandering from clime to clime" a few lines later.

title: Frankenstein and "Elementary"
description: Frankenstein is the creator, not the creature; and Holmes never says "Elementary, my dear Watson" in Conan Doyle's stories.

facts.text: In Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818), Frankenstein is Victor Frankenstein, a scientist who artificially creates a human being.
The Folger Shakespeare Library calls it one of the enduring confusions of Frankenstein that the name belongs not to the Creature but to his creator.

"Elementary, my dear Watson" is not found in any of Conan Doyle's stories; the nearest is "Excellent!" I cried. "Elementary," said he. in The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, and the misquotation is first recorded in P. G. Wodehouse's Psmith, Journalist.
Holmes occasionally calls his conclusions "elementary" and often addresses his friend as "my dear Watson".

title: The Shakespeare authorship theories
description: Doubts about Shakespeare began in the 1800s; the Oxford theory (1920) founders on Oxford's death in 1604, and mainstream scholars reject it.

facts.text: For over 200 years after Shakespeare's death, nobody questioned that he wrote his works; doubts arose in the Victorian era, when Delia Bacon argued that Francis Bacon wrote the plays.
J. Thomas Looney proposed in 1920 that Edward de Vere, earl of Oxford, wrote the plays; but Oxford died in 1604, and by standard dating more than a dozen plays were written after that.
Historians and literary scholars overwhelmingly reject the alternative authorship candidates, including Oxford.
In the First Folio (1623), Ben Jonson called Shakespeare the "Sweet Swan of Avon", tying the writer to Stratford-upon-Avon.

title: What makes a classic
description: Twain joked that a classic is praised and not read; Calvino answered that a classic never runs out of things to say and carries the traces of earlier readings.

facts.text: In Following the Equator (1897), Mark Twain defined a classic as "A book which people praise and don't read."
In his essay "Why Read the Classics?", Italo Calvino called a classic a book that never finishes saying what it has to say.

title: Three questions for placing a classic
description: Calvino's traces suggest three questions for any classic: where it comes from, how it works and what others have taken from it; tried on Gilgamesh.

facts.text: Calvino also wrote that the classics come down to us bearing traces of the readings before ours, and of the marks they have left on languages and customs.
